subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang_ (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has already been indicated in the House on several occasions that it is the intention of the government to conduct a poll of rapeseed growers in western Canada before the end of the year to determine the system they prefer for the marketing of their product. On June 1, I announced the appointment of a supervisor for the poll, Mr. George S. Turner, to take charge of the task of consulting with rapeseed growers and overseeing the conduct of the poll itself. On the basis of Mr. Turner's consultations with growers and their organizations the following criteria for the conduct of the poll were recommended and accepted by government:
1.	A producer eligible to vote in the poll will be defined as a Canadian Wheat Board regular permit holder whose permit indicates acreage seeded to rapeseed in any two out of the three crop years, 1971-72, 1972-73 and 1973-74. Also eligible to vote will be new permit holders who grew grain for the first time in 1972 or 1973 and whose permit books indicate acreage seeded to rapeseed in at least one year.
2.	The ballot will be worded so that the rapeseed grower may indicate his preference for one of two options for the marketing of his rapeseed, that is, the present system or the Canadian Wheat Board, plus the opportunity to register an undecided vote.
3.	A majority of at least 60 per cent of the ballots returned must be in favour of the Canadian Wheat Board alternative before such a change could be made.
4.	Ballots will be mailed to producers in early December, 1973.
Information concerning alternative marketing systems for rapeseed will be distributed to growers prior to the poll to assist them in deciding on the system they prefer for
the marketing of their product. Manitoba Pool Elevators, Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and Alberta Wheat Pool, at our request, have jointly prepared an information brochure stating the case for including the marketing of rapeseed under the Canadian Wheat Board. The Rapeseed Association of Canada, again at our invitation, has prepared a brochure stating the case for the open market method of rapeseed marketing. The pools and the rapeseed association have borne the cost of preparing the material for their respective brochures while the government is bearing the cost of printing and distributing the material. The brochures will be jointly mailed on November 16 to those rapeseed growers who are eligible to vote in the poll. The ballots will be mailed on December 3 and voters will have until December 14 to return their ballots to the supervisor of the poll, Mr. George S. Turner. The results of the poll will be made known to the House immediately following the conclusion of the poll.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by thanking the minister responsible for the Wheat Board for sending us a copy of his statement a few minutes before he rose to make the statement in the House. It is a good idea for the government and various organizations to keep farmers well informed, and it was a good idea for the minister to make the kind of statement he made today well in advance of the intended rapeseed plebiscite.
The vote that will take place in the first part of December will be most important. A great many people see it as possibly a turning point for agriculture in Canada in relation to the Wheat Board form of marketing, which is basically negotiation and the pooling of prices, as against the concept of futures marketing in which prices are determined by supply and demand in the marketplace at any given time. There have been requests by organizations to postpone the plebiscite because of the complexity of the task of explaining the differences between open or futures marketing method and the Wheat Board selling method. The minister did not allude to this, but I understand they have been turned down and the vote will be taking place in the first part of December.
I am glad to see that in the plebiscite there will be an opportunity to register undecided votes. I take it from the minister's remarks that undecided votes will be counted as votes for retention of the present futures marketing system for rapeseed and flax.
When one looks at the whole situation concerning rape-seed and the tremendous growth of this crop over the past few years under the futures or open marketing system it is obvious that the growth has been phenomenal. I believe that for a good many producers across western Canada it has been a very satisfactory way of selling their product.

October 26, 1973
Rapeseed Plebiscite
While it might be improper for us as politicians to get involved at this time on one side or the other inasmuch as this is a good opportunity to let the issue be decided by the growers associations and the people directly involved in the plebiscite, I hasten to say that when one looks at the whole situation at the present time it seems that the present method of marketing rapeseed is quite satisfactory.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one looks at the statement made by the minister on the question of the rapeseed marketing poll one wonders how far the government is going in the direction of government by plebiscite. It seems strange that when there is an issue whether this commodity should be sold on the open market or marketed by the Canadian Wheat Board we suddenly have a plebiscite. Where is the plebiscite on the action taken with regard to feed grains? There is none.
If 51 per cent of the producers who return the forms say they want the Canadian Wheat Board to market their rapeseed, it will not be done. If 59 per cent say that is what they want, it will not be done. The plebiscite requires 60 per cent. That must be what is called Liberal democracy. The question should be decided on the basis of a simple majority one way or the other. If a 60 per cent majority were required to form a government in this country, we would not have a government at this time.

speechtext: The Conservative critic stated, as the Tories have done with regard to every major policy that has come before the House, that they want a hands off policy. They do not want to take a stand. Not taking a stand in the debate that will take place on rapeseed simply means one thing, a stand for an open market. All members of the House should take a stand. In fact, the minister should take a stand. Where do the politicians stand in regard to marketing rapeseed? This party stands for putting flax, rye and rapeseed under the jursidiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL
speechtext:
Under the open market system farmers sign contracts for $3 a bushel and the brokers and shysters resell the rapeseed at $6 to $7 a bushel. I say it is time we moved into a position of orderly marketing through the Canadian Wheat Board.
The leaders of the farm organizations and the members of the government should state where they stand. It is nonsensical to hold a poll now when last year the government brought in amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act which raised the question of the marketing of these commodities outside that board. The New Democratic Party moved an amendment in committee to the Wheat Board Act to provide for the marketing of flax, rye and rapeseed under the jurisdiction of the board. The government party and the Official Opposition defeated that amendment. Now there is to be a plebiscite and the law does not even allow the Wheat Board to market these

grains even if the farmers vote in favour of the proposition.
Does the minister in charge of the Wheat Board give western farmers the assurance that if they vote for Wheat Board marketing his colleagues will allow him to bring such an amendment before the House? Will the Conservative party allow the government to give the Wheat Board jurisdiction over rapeseed? I think the manner in which the plebiscite has been set up, and the manner in which the government is carrying it out, amounts to an attempt to weigh the procedure in favour of the open market system.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CRITERIA FOR CONDUCTING RAPESEED MARKETING POLL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the minister's statement that a consultation of producers would be held in late November or early December is an undertaking to enable an important area of our economy to express itself and choose a process for the marketing of its production.
As stated in paragraph (2) of the minister's statement, the ballot will be worded so that the rapeseed grower may indicate his preference for one of two options for the marketing of his rapeseed, that is, the present system or the Canadian Wheat Board, plus the opportunity to register an undecided vote.
Mr. Speaker, this process seems to me altogether democratic and enables producers to choose their own marketing system for their products. I understand that in other fields of production, they do not operate this way and I would suggest that the Department apply that consultation policy not merely to rapeseed growers but also to all other Canadian farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has Canada in fact been requested by the Secretary General of the United Nations to contribute to the peacekeeping force being sent to the Middle East war zone as a consequence of yesterday's Security Council resolution and, if so, what is the response of the government?

October 26, 1973

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary o£ State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST TO CANADA TO CONTRIBUTE TO MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE, INCREASE CYPRUS UNIT OR PARTICIPATION IN UNTSO
speechtext: The answer to the question is no. The Secretary General has not as yet asked Canada to contribute any forces. It is my understanding he is calling upon the traditional neutral countries, Sweden, Finland and Austria, which have troops ready and available in Cyprus, to make the initial contribution.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST TO CANADA TO CONTRIBUTE TO MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE, INCREASE CYPRUS UNIT OR PARTICIPATION IN UNTSO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister if the transfer of Austrian, Finnish and Swedish troops to the Middle East zone has caused a consequent request to Canada for alteration or augmentation of our force in that peacekeeping group?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST TO CANADA TO CONTRIBUTE TO MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE, INCREASE CYPRUS UNIT OR PARTICIPATION IN UNTSO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have not yet received such a request. If it were made we would, I think, look at it sympathetically if this were a way to help establish a peacekeeping force in the Middle East. We would want to be sure, however, that the peacekeeping force in Cyprus would remain a truly international force. It would not be our wish to change the character of that peacekeeping force in any way.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST TO CANADA TO CONTRIBUTE TO MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE, INCREASE CYPRUS UNIT OR PARTICIPATION IN UNTSO
speechtext: I have one final supplementary, Mr. Speaker, with reference to a statement by the minister yesterday, I believe. Have we been asked to supplement or augment our UNTSO contribution?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST TO CANADA TO CONTRIBUTE TO MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE, INCREASE CYPRUS UNIT OR PARTICIPATION IN UNTSO
speechtext: Not yet. It is my understanding that the Secretary General will be announcing the terms of reference of that peacekeeping force at three o'clock this afternoon, at which time the situation may be a little clearer.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, October 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-164, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system and Air Canada for the period from the 1st day of January, 1973 to the 30th day of June, 1974 , and securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company and certain debentures to be issued by Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that it will come as no surprise to the members of this House when I say that I intend to devote my remarks in this second reading debate on Bill C-164, having to do with the financing of Canadian National Railways and Air Canada, to one subject, pensions. Towards the end of my remarks, I shall make a few
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada comments about the pension package that has been agreed on in the collective bargaining process. That has now gone to arbitration. In the main, however, I want to concentrate on the position of retired railway workers; in other words, those out of service, those now on their pensions.
When we raise questions about retired railway workers, Canadian National and Canadian Pacific, we get certain stock answers. One of those answers is that the whole question of pensions has at long last been put on the collective bargaining table and that we should not, therefore, be discussing it on the floor of the House of Commons. I remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who is one of those who gives us this stock answer, that the retired railway workers were not represented at the collective bargaining table and that the arrangements arrived at in the process of collective bargaining relating to pensions did not provide anything at all for those already retired.
There is nothing new about this situation. A few years ago, when the question of Canadian National pensions was before the appropriate standing committee, many witnesses appeared before the committee. Some of them were retired railways workers who, in their working days, had been general chairmen of their unions. They admitted to us that when they were general chairmen and giving leadership to and working on behalf of their unions their main interest centered on those who were working. In those days they did not express any great concern, if, indeed, they expressed any concern at all, about those already retired.
When those same general chairmen joined the group of workers who are retired and tried to live on their pensions, their viewpoint was quite different. Clearly, the situation is not a new one. It is one that this House ought to face. The position of retired railway workers, those already on pension, does not get adequate consideration in the normal collective bargaining process, and thus it is our responsibility to speak on their behalf on the floor of the House of Commons.
I wish to point out also that the few times when we have secured something for the retired employees of Canadian National Railways, and in an ancillary way for employees of other railways, it has come about because of debate in parliament, either on the floor of the House or in the standing committee. Each time something has been done to improve the pensions of retired railway workers, the announcement has been made by the president of Canadian National Railways or in the case of Canadian Pacific, by the president of that organization, but the activity that brought about those changes took place on the floor of this House of Commons or in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I feel it is our duty as members of parliament, and most of us in this House represent railway workers or retired railway workers, some a few and some of us many, to speak for those for whom the case is not made when the collective bargaining process takes place.
I know that in the revised setup of the board that administers Canadian National pensions, there is one representative of those who have retired, but that does not

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada seem to be the place where policy is made. That seems to be a place where administration is supervised. The fact is that in terms of the policy for those now working, it is a matter that is dealt with at the collective bargaining table. For those already retired, the only way their voice can be heard is by forming their own organizations, issuing press releases, writing members of parliament and so on, or by our stating their case on the floor of parliament. That is the reason I choose in this debate on Bill C-164 to direct all of my remarks to the question of pensions and, as I say, mainly to the position of those already retired.
It is sometimes suggested to us that one reason we should leave this subject alone is that the question of railway pensions has been given to Dr. John Deutsch, who was recently appointed as a commissioner by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). May I remind hon. members of the limitations imposed on Dr. Deutsch. He has not been given a commission to study the whole question of railway pensions. His commission is only to assess the monetary value of the pension package agreed to at the bargaining table. The railway companies put a certain value on it in percentage terms. The unions put a lower percentage value on it. All that Dr. Deutsch is commissioned to do is arrive at a fair evaluation of the pension package and if it is different from what has been submitted by the companies, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall is to take that into consideration in the final award arising out of the rail dispute of last summer.
When the appointment of Dr. Deutsch was announced in this House by the Minister of Labour, some of us pleaded for his terms of reference to be enlarged to include an examination of the railway pension plans in their entirety or, alternatively, for another commissioner to be appointed to look into that broader question. The Minister of Labour expressed some interest. In fact, I think it is fair to say he agreed this should be done, but he pleaded that now was not the time to do it,-

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: It never is.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
-that we should first wait for the job to be done by Dr. Deutsch. As my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Co wichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), interjected a moment ago, the time never is right to do something like this.
A commission similar to that given to Dr. Deutsch should be given to him or some other competent or impartial person to go into the whole question of the fairness of railway pension plans. In my view, such a commission should not only include the fairness or otherwise of the plan to which working railway employees are now contributing, but the fairness of the plan in the way it treats retired employees. In any event, I submit these two answers that are given to us, first that pensions are the subject of collective bargaining and, second, that Dr. Deutsch has been appointed as a commissioner, do not touch at all on the problem and the plight of retired railway workers who are already on pension, for whom there is nothing in the new pension package and whose case is not to be considered under Dr. Deutsch's commission.
With regard to railway workers already retired, the first thing that must be done, and frankly I think that any

delay on this is completely unforgiveable, is that the escalation of railway pensions should be put on a basis equal to that which has now been accorded to old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, the pensions of retired public servants and of armed forces and ROMP personnel, pensions and allowances awarded to veterans and soon, because the appropriate bill is now before the House, on pensions paid under the Canada Pension Plan. The day of a 2 per cent ceiling on the annual escalation of pensions should end. It is over for all those groups I have just named. It should be ended completely.
I submit the government does have responsibility for the Canadian National Railways. It should say right now that just as there is no longer a 2 per cent ceiling on the escalation of pensions for federal public employees and a whole host of other persons whose pensions come under the responsibility of the federal government, there should no longer be imposed a 2 per cent ceiling on the annual escalation of railway pensions, either Canadian National or Canadian Pacific.
One of the arguments the railways have advanced against an escalation of higher than 2 per cent is and has been for some time that they were not allowed to do so by the law. Unfortunately, that statement is correct. There was a section in the income tax regulations which denied registration for the purpose of income tax deductibility to any company whose private pension plan provided for an escalation greater than 2 per cent per year. However, that has been changed. Only a few days ago the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Stanbury) circulated an information bulletin in which it is made clear that this ceiling no longer applies. The new regulation says a pension plan can be registered and can qualify for tax deductibility provided any escalation is not greater than the actual percentage increase in the cost of living. The door has been opened wide. Canadian National now faces no barrier whatever against escalating the pensions of its retired employees on the same basis as all government pensions. I urge and insist that this be done. I do not intend to be put down by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) saying this is not the place in which to discuss this matter. It does not get discussed anywhere else. In the past, efforts of ours in the House of Commons or in the standing committee have produced an effect. Our purpose in pressing this issue now is to make the government realize it must tell the CNR to match what the federal government has done in this area. I would point out that the escalation of all the pensions I listed a few moments ago, from old age security right down to the Canada Pensions Plan bill that is now on the order paper, whether annual or quarterly as in the case of the guaranteed income supplement and old age security payments, is provided for by law. It is automatic. It takes place without any question. Not so in the case of CNR pensions. The CNR has on three or four occasions made escalation benefits available at the rate of 2 per cent a year. But this was done out of the goodness of the company's heart. I suggest it should be automatic-it should be made part of the pension rules, part of the regulations, so that retired employees can count on an escalation every year without question. They ought not have to depend on a meeting of the pension board or of the directors of CN reaching a decision that this should be done. It should be automatic,
October 26, 1973

and the escalation should be made equal to the actual increase in the cost of living. I want to see this provision put into the plan for the future, for those who are presently working. They are pressing for it, and I support them in that effort. But as far as those who are already retired are concerned, nobody speaks for them unless we do so here. I am doing so today, as I have done so often, because I want to see action taken.
I argue, too, on behalf of those workers who are already retired, that they have a case for the recalculation of the basis of their pensions. It is certainly better to calculate the escalation on the basis of the actual cost of living increase rather than on a basis of 2 per cent but when one is dealing with pensions which start at very low levels, percentage increases often mean very little. Some change in the formula is coming about. The package worked out at the bargaining table includes a new formula but nothing in that formula applies to those already retired. A recalculation of the basis of the pension paid to all retired employees should underpin the amount of the escalation for which I have been arguing.
A third point I press is the unfairness of a pension system under which a widow's pension is only 50 per cent of what her husband would have received. I know this situation arises out of a deep, dark, mythological past when it seemed right to retire a man on a pension of 100 per cent even though his wife had predeceased him, but expect the widow to get by on 50 per cent. I think pensions should be paid on an equal basis across the board, though at the moment I am concentrating on the case of retired railway workers. I think the time has come to increase that figure of 50 per cent. In my view the pension should be the same for either spouse. I do not see why, when the man is the one who survives, he should get 100 per cent though the woman, if she survives, gets only 50 per cent. After all, they each helped to do the work and provide the pension. It is, really, their pension, not just his. This is a concept I have raised a number of times and I intend to continue to do so. The least we should insist on is that just as our widows, the widows of Members of Parliament, will get 60 per cent of our pensions the widows of railway workers should also get 60 per cent. I think it should be more than this. I think it should be at least 75 per cent. In any case, this is one of the things which in my view should be adjusted, and, to begin with it should be adjusted in the case of widows of those who have already retired.
Because Bill C-164 refers to Canadian National Railways I have, of course, talked mainly about CN pensions, as is necessary if I am to stay in order. But I have made the odd reference to the Canadian Pacific pension plan and I should like to point out now that if there are deficiencies in the Canadian National plan there are far worse deficiencies in the CP plan. I emphasize in particular that its escalation provisions do nothing at all for the old-timers who retired before 1956. Indeed, even for many of those who retired after 1956, no credit is given for escalation purposes for service prior to 1956, the result being that the escalation benefits some of these old-time employees get is in terms of dimes or quarters, not in dollars. I think it is scandalous that a company which has
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada received so much from the government and the people of Canada should be able to get away with this sort of thing.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
I said I would concentrate on the case of those who have already retired, and I have done so, partly, as I say, because there is no one to speak for them unless we do so, and partly because this is the place where we can put pressure on the government to put pressure on the railways. To summarize, I believe we should press for action on three main points: first, an escalation formula equal to the rise in the cost of living as is the case with federal pensions; second, that this should be provided in the rules or regulations instead of leaving it at the mercy of management; third, the percentage paid to the widows of retired railway employees should be increased.
I should now like to say a few words about the package which has been agreed to by management and the unions. I suppose I should choose my words carefully because these terms have been agreed upon at the collective bargaining table as part of the total deal which will come out of the arbitration being conducted by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall. However, I must say I hope this agreement is not the end of the story as far as railway pensions are concerned. I am talking, now, about those in the service. There is an improvement. They are to get a 2 per cent formula for some years of their service and a somewhat better deal in case of early retirement; in othe- words, workers can retire early without a severe penalty; those who have served for a time beyond what the new package allows for will be permitted to enjoy that extra credit. But it seems to me there are very real deficiencies in the plan which has been accepted.
For one thing, there is nothing at all in this package to benefit anyone who retired prior to January 1, 1973. Even those who retire after January 1, 1973, will find that that new pension package does not change by one cent the credit they get for their service prior to 1956. The idea was that the time had come for a 2 per cent pension, a 2 per cent credit for every year of service in the way the public service pension plan operates and also Air Canada's. Instead, we have a one per cent, a 1.5 or 2 per cent pension for a few years, or a 1.3 per cent scheme integrated with the Canada Pension Plan, and so on. But we do not have an across the board 2 per cent per year of service formula which I think must yet be incorporated into the pension plans of railway workers.
I do not like the way in which the integration between the railway pensions and the Canada Pension Plan has been built up. As a matter of act, I think it was a mistake right from the start that the Canada Pension Plan was not stacked or decked in the case of railway workers, and many railway workers feel that out of this deal they are not getting the kind of terms of benefits that they ought to get.
I said that there is nothing in the package to cover any service prior to 1956. That means that older workers in our railway systems who are still working and had a fair amount of service prior to 1956 will not get a pension that
7266

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
is much better under this package than if the package had not been agreed to at all.
I am deliberately keeping my remarks with respect to that part of the deal brief because it is the subject of collective bargaining, as I say, and it is up to the parties to fight it out. But I make the suggestion that they should press hard for a 2 per cent formula across the board. I think they should press for absolutely no penalties on early retirement, they should press for the Canada Pension Plan to be stacked instead of integrated, and they should press for an equal pension for the widow as for the employee when either one of them is bereaved.
I feel very strongly that those who are still in service and are represented through their unions should press for improvements of that kind in their pension plan; and of course they should press for the full escalation of their pensions after they retire in accordance with the actual rise in the cost of living. I offer this advice to those in service who are still trying to build up their pensions to what they ought to be, and they know they have my full support.
I close by pleading with the House to tell this government to instruct the Canadian National Railways-and it can talk to the CPR too; after all, that railway owes a great deal to this place-that the time has come, so far as railway workers already retired are concerned, for their pensions to be escalated by the actual increase in the cost of living; that it is time for recalculation of their basic pensions in line with an improved formula; and that it is time for widows of these workers to get a much better deal than the 50 per cent pension now provided. I hope that our keeping this debate going a bit longer to press these points will have its effect and that the government will realize that members of all sides of the House want a fair deal for our retired railway workers, including those who worked for the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific and all the rest of this country's railways.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill has been before the House for a year or so now. When it was first introduced, ministers did address themselves to it. I would hope that hon. members, all of whose points have been very carefully noted by the government, would find the committee a very useful procedure not only for calling ministers to answer questions but also the executives of the railway.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that the minister would indicate on his point of order that he was in fact prepared to participate, but it seems he is not. I would remind him that, while there have been other bills relating to CNR financing in other years which were not completed, this particular bill was introduced in March and, as I say, was moved and debated on April 13.
The specific issues to which I want to address myself have relation to the recent railway strike which took place in the latter part of August of this year which had a very detrimental impact on two Canadian provinces in particular and, of course, on all provinces in general. During the course of the debate on the special legislation that was enacted to put the railroads back into service, namely on August 31, I raised the question of the increasing frequency of ferry tie-ups as a direct result of a national rail strike, the first in 1950, the second in 1966 and the third this year, 1973.
Tragically for the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, all of these strikes occurred at the peak travel and tourist time,-I think tourism in both provinces is now the second or third largest industry- tying up ferries for a considerable number of days during the month of August. I would, therefore, be remiss in my duty as one representative from Prince Edward Island if I did not continue to press, immediately following the resolution of the work stoppage that occurred in August, for a procedure that would be implemented by CNR, in concert with the government, that would insure against, or at least would give the strongest possible assurance against, such disruption in the future.
As I said during the debate on August 31 and in subsequent correspondence both with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the Minister of Transport, ferry service to Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland can only be regarded as essential. Indeed, it has been regarded as
October 26, 1973

essential since confederation, both the confederation of a century ago in the case of Prince Edward Island and the confederation of one quarter of a century ago in the case of Newfoundland. Written into the terms of confederation in both instances is the iron-clad guarantee by the federal government that there shall be no interruption, no break whatsoever, in the kind of communication and transportation that is necessary for a province to function effectively within the Canadian framework. I think it is regrettable that this party presently in power, having experienced in three successive instances such a major dislocation of transportation facilities to and from our island provinces, should not have acted effectively to introduce measures either following the 1950 strike, the 1966 strike or the 1973 strike to insure the people of our island provinces against any further disastrous disruptions.
At the time of the debate on the legislation to end the rail strike, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), particularly because he was at that time piloting the special legislation, whether he would take firm action following the immediate crisis to convene a meeting at the highest level. Perhaps I may read again the comment I made on August 31 to be found at page 6143 of Hansard:
All I am saying to the Minister of Labour at this point is that now we have to realize, having gone through this situation three times since 1950, that we must not put these two provinces in the same jeopardy again. In order to achieve that purpose I think the minister must give an undertaking that in the course of the next few months we will work out a new structure which will prevent the same situation from occurring again, not in total terms because we know we cannot prevent it in total terms, but to go a good deal beyond the present situation which is merely a bandaid approach.
The Minister of Labour, if I may quote him, responded to me at that point and is recorded here as having said:
I hope to achieve that.
Following that verbal commitment in the House on that date, I wrote a more detailed letter to the Minister of Labour, copies of which I sent to a number of people mentioned in the letter, particularly those directly responsible such as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), the premiers of both Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, the executive of the Canadian National Railways and the representatives of the various union brotherhoods directly affected. I asked the Minister of Labour, again because he had taken the primary role in piloting the legislation related to the immediate strike difficulties, whether he would convene a meeting to be held with the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Transport, the Hon. Jean Marchand, Premier Frank Moores of Newfoundland, Premier Alexander Campbell of Prince Edward Island, plus representatives of the appropriate unions and the Canadian National Railway.
As I said in the letter:
I believe that you are amenable to this suggestion. I am hopeful, therefore, that plans for such a meeting are going ahead.
I received an acknowledgment of that letter some weeks following indicating that the minister felt that primarily it was not his reponsibility but that of his colleague the Minister of Transport. I sent a copy of that letter to the Minister of Transport, and subsequently wrote the Minis-
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada ter of Transport directly, as well as the Premier of my own province of Prince Edward Island in which letter I again advanced the importance of a high-level meeting to resolve this recurring difficulty. In addition, I put on the table one specific proposal whereby the situation might be resolved. I am going to mention that proposal in a moment so it can be on the record of this House and, hopefully, so there can be some comment not only from the Minister of Transport but perhaps from other members either in this House or on the committee in respect of some workable formula.
We are in a difficult situation. We have increasingly enacted legislation in this country to provide free collective bargaining for almost every employee in every industry, except those in the very few services thought to be so essential to the public interest it is not considered wise or fair to the general public to grant such rights. In the course of developing our transportation system, certain collective bargaining arrangements which have been achieved by railway employees have affected directly the operations of our car-ferry system, and this has resulted in the loss of an essential service three times in the last two decades.
We are now faced with having to try to reconcile what, at the outset, seems irreconcilable: How can we operate a modern essential car-ferry link between the two island provinces, assuring that service through all kinds of various labour disputes and disruptions, without either taking some chance with the general public welfare and interest or adopting restrictive measures in respect of the car-ferry employees? This is not an easy problem to resolve and if anyone suggests it is he would, I think, be extremely superficial about the nature of the difficulties.
In recent days the premier of Prince Edward Island has advanced the proposition that what we now need is a Crown corporation. He has been somewhat unclear as to whether this would simply be a provincial Crown corporation or a federal one, but he suggests that such a Crown corporation would be mandated to operate the car-ferry services and its employees would essentially be prohibited from having the right to strike. This would be for many a reversal of the current development of labour relations within governmental departments, agencies and Crown corporations. While such action may be popularly received by a large segment of the general public, it would not be considered to be a very progressive approach toward those who would be employed by such a Crown corporation.
If such legislation came before us in the House of Commons, we would certainly be faced with passing legislation that would, in a sense, be a backward step from the direction in which we have been moving, in addition to which it is not entirely clear that in establishing a separate entity we would in fact be providing better or improved transportation services to the island provinces. Nor is it clear that to those directly employed we would be providing them with the most fair and just employee framework possible. Until we know a great deal more about this proposal, I think at the outset it would seem to have a considerable number of difficulties related to it. Other questions have been raised about the possibility of the ministry of transport directly operating a car-ferry
7268

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada system, but until we solve these rights of the employees we really have not in any way escaped the essential issues.
On March 9 I wrote a letter both to the Minister of Transport and to the Premier of Prince Edward Island, again suggesting that a meeting should be convened at the earliest possible moment in respect of this problem, but more than that suggesting that I should like to put on the table for serious consideration one possibility of overcoming the increasing frequency of these disastrous car-ferry tie-ups.
What I suggested, and I will quote largely from the correspondence, is that a contingency plan be prepared within the next few months jointly by the Canadian National Railways, the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence, and that this contingency plan would provide for a special operation procedure to be instituted by the Canadian armed forces in the event of a labour walkout that would tie up the car-ferry system. I suggested that this plan should be capable of being instituted in a very short time period, within 24 to 48 hours, that the obvious seafaring capabilities within the armed forces be made use of and that the men and other resources necessary to effect this alternate operation would be adjacent to the ferry system so that problems of transportation and the allocating of a number of employees would not be all that difficult.
This would satisfy the first and perhaps most major concern, that is of providing continuous ferry service. It would also allow employees to use their full rights in a bargaining sense and, if the whole process of negotiation broke down, to in fact have a walkout. They would, of course, in any walkout be penalized in the sense they would no longer be drawing their regular rates of pay. Such strike pay as would be available to them would be of some assistance, but they would suffer the usual penalties on a personal basis from going out on strike.
The essential difficulty in this proposal would be the fact that with car-ferries continuing in operation there would be no great direct pressure on the railway company itself to achieve a speedy settlement to the dispute. Therefore, I also suggested that when a work stoppage occurred, and the Canadian armed forces were called in, the Canadian National Railways would experience two direct penalties. The first would be that the normal day-to-day revenues they would receive during the period that the ferries would be operated by this alternate manpower would not go to the CNR but would return to the federal treasury. This would mean a deprivation to the extent of some thousands of dollars, depending on the length of time the strike was in effect.
Second, and perhaps most importantly in terms of the economic pressure on the CNR, I suggested that the annual subsidy which now runs into millions of dollars would be pro-rated during the strike period, and that that amount of money would be withdrawn as an additional penalty thus providing a stronger economic pressure on the railway to effect a speedy settlement of the dispute. I realize that this is a somewhat different approach to the problem and one which requires the assistance of other departments. It would set in play a different kind of

operation. However, I have been intrigued to note to date that there has been no extensive criticism, no suggestion that there is a fundamental weakness in the proposition, although I am quite prepared to consider such fundamental objections and, indeed, would not want such a plan to be implemented until it had the most thorough kind of scrutiny.
It would seem to me this, at least, is one possibility for ensuring the continuation of service between the province of Prince Edward Island and the mainland, as well as continuing basic employee rights within the framework of the present car-ferry operation as operated by the Canadian National Railways. If we are to have some proposal in which all interested parties are included, the employer, the employees and the two levels of government, I believe now is the time for the officials in the railway company, along with governmental representatives, to get together in an effort to directly face some of these problems.
We have been told there has been some form of communication between some of the people directly involved, but it is quite obvious to us that there has been no serious meeting of minds between the federal officials responsible and the government of the province of Prince Edward Island. I would say, and I hope this is not an indication of the current state of the CNR, that the Canadian National is about the only interested party which has not yet replied to either of my two letters concerning this major difficulty. Since this company has a basic responsibility to operate the ferry service on a day-to-day basis it would seem that this should be a fundamental concern to it. Certainly, the suggestions I have advanced, with the penalty which would be involved should another car-ferry tie-up occur in the near future, could involve an amount of some tens of hundreds or thousands of dollars. If the Canadian National should have a modification of the proposal I have produced, I would hope they would place it on the table fairly quickly.
I believe the citizens of our country in the two island provinces will not accept again the kind of difficulties from which they have not yet even now, two months after the strike, fully recovered. It is not possible to say either in economic or human terms the difficulty created for those two provinces. There is a responsibility upon the CN and the two levels of government to work out an acceptable procedure to prevent this happening again.
I wish to make one or two further comments because I think they are important in respect of the transportation problems of Prince Edward Island. In particular, I wish to speak about the ferry system that is operating there which resumed operation following this recent strike. I think we are rapidly approaching another time of great difficulty in respect of the continuous transportation of both passengers, goods and heavy equipment to and from the province. It is a well known fact that since roughly the Second World War we have had only two car ferries capable of handling the freight and traffic to and from the province, the Abegweit, which is now 25 years of age, and until recently the John Hamilton Gray.
We know that the Abegweit, which has been a very efficient railway car ferry, is coming to the point of needing a major refit in the very near future. We have been told for the past two or three years that it has been
October 26, 1973

operating at slower than normal speed. We know it would not take too much to put it out of service for a considerable length of time. For the total kind of refit and overhaul required, it would need to be out of service for at least a year. That would be an impossible situation because the other car ferry, while built originally for Prince Edward Island, has operated on a half-year basis serving the province of Newfoundland.
We islanders are patient and understanding people, and know that our fellow islanders in Newfoundland have similar and sometimes greater transportation difficulties. However, we think it inconceivable that we should be faced in the next year or so with a situation in which our basic ferry should finally go out of service, and that the other car ferry might be off some hundred miles away serving the province of Newfoundland. This government must make a commitment now with the Canadian National Railways and with the Department of Transport to provide a car-rail carrying ferry service that can, in effect, ensure that the basic goods, particularly the most basic commodity of all in terms of the agricultural industry, potatoes, are transported on a regular basis.
I was impressed by a recent report of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which met in Prince Edward Island this past June. It recommended that the Maritime Provinces Chamber of Commerce continue to prevail upon the Government of Canada the urgent need for a new, modern ice-breaking ferry to serve between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick as soon as possible. I shall not read the preamble because of the shortness of time, but I think it is incumbent on the government with the CNR to make, within the next few months, a definite commitment so that Prince Edward Island will not find itself again in a situation of totally inadequate transportation facilities for the movement of its basic goods and services.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this endless debate on the CNR-Air Canada financing bill C-164, I would like to speak in a very general way about something that is obviously basic to a country such as Canada. The paradox in the development of Canada was that, in spite of the problem which transportation presented, it was transportation through the CPR which finally welded us together from coast to coast. In that very paradox, we are brought face to face with the problems of present day Canada for it is the lack of transportation in this modern day of technology, of computers and of science which we have at our disposal,
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada that is creating some of the fundamental problems in this country. I wonder, as we deliberate on the CNR-Air Canada financing bill which gives hon. members a chance to speak in both a general and a specific way about transportation and about Air Canada and CNR in particular, whether anyone in positions of authority in CNR, Air Canada or the CTC will be listening and, I hope, reacting to some of the concrete proposals that have been put forward during this debate.
I, personally, believe that what the western premiers tried to do last July at the western economic conference, which now is more or less forgotten because of the other problems that have flowed swiftly thereafter-as my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) says, there has been much flowing but there have been a few bumps along the way and in the result we are all shaken up a little-was to convince Ottawa that transportation should become an instrument of the national development policy for the regions of Canada. This would seem to me to be almost axiomatic in a place like Canada and something with which a federal government exercising federal leadership should agree. To put it in another way, a provision should be included in the National Transportation Act that transportation should become the instrument for development for the regions. Of course, if you develop the regions and give them strength, you will have a stronger country.
I really could not understand the reluctance of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand)-who unfortunately is away this afternoon, but I gather he has been absent for the greater part of this debate-to accept this fundamental principle. After all, it was a man called Macdonald, who is popularly called the father of this country, who developed the national policy on various tariffs and rates which helped in building the central core of this country and helped to define the boundaries of the country above the 49th parallel. We had a policy that developed this country, and now all that the west and the east, and I think even some people in the central part of Canada, are asking for is that an attempt be made to redress the balance that is somewhat out of kilter because of the over concentration and development of the industry in the central core of Canada, by including the principle in the National Transportation Act that transportation should be a tool of national development. The fact that the federal government could not go along with that very basic premise concerns me.
The National Transportation Act was only passed in 1967 and it is based on compensatory rates. You are supposed to get from the shipper only what he is willing to pay, or in other words, you are supposed to do away with subsidies over a long period of time. I will have more to say about subsidies in a minute. Can you have transportation as a tool for regional or national economic development, and on the other hand, as is presently written in the National Transportation Act, agree with the principle that transportation should be based on compensatory rates? I think that in many parts of this country, in so far as the passenger service is concerned but even more with regard to the freight service, rail transportation is fundamental to the growth of the region. It may be that the compensatory rate that the railway would like to charge is going to be too high, and almost too confiscatory for that industry or

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada that part of the country to grow. I think there has to be a review of the Transportation Act to try to balance transportation as a tool of economic development against the present section in the act which provides that transportation must only flow on the basis of compensatory rates.
Here, we have the irony of debating the CN financing bill with all the mythology of rates that was built into the infrastructure of CN financing, especially in the forties and fifties, and the refinancing of their capitalization which was supposed to do away with subsidies or grants from the government. We have this paradox. There was a great teacher around the Sea of Galilee many, many years ago who taught in parables. I think the political scene in Canada can almost be taught in paradoxes. You can see the political fabric of our country and coming to transportation there is a paradox that we all know. The strike last summer brought it home again. It is that although rail may not be the most popular mode of transportation for passengers service, railroads are fundamental to growth. Balanced against that is the compensatory rate structure that is built into the national transportation system, and which I say is not helping to develop the economy of the country.
In trying to revise the principle of the Transportation Act to make it a tool of economic development, I do not suggest that the taxpayer of Canada should be asked to subsidize inefficient forms of transportation. As members of parliament and the transportation committee, whether the CN, the CP or any other group came before the Transport and Communications Committee, we should be looking for ways to make the railway system more efficient rather than doing what is so easily done, and that is letting the taxpayer pay because in the end the money comes out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This is what other governments have done, and it is just subsidizing the inefficiencies of the system. We should be looking at transportation as a tool of economic development, and not using the criteria that the railways can charge what the shipper can bear. Let us change the system and make it more efficient rather than perpetuating its distortions, inadequacies and inefficiencies.
I will give some precise example of the inadequacies of the present system, Mr. Speaker. On the east coast, as Your Honour and other members from the east coast and central Canada are aware, we have a container port where the ships of the world bring their container traffic. There they are supposed to be loaded on to unit trains which, in theory and to a degree in practice, flow through the heartland of the United States and Canada. You would think that this would have brought unremitting loud hosannas from all Canadians, let alone those in Atlantic Canada.
But, Mr. Speaker, while the container facilities have been of value to the export shipper or the import shipper and of some benefit to Atlantic Canada, they have not necessarily been of benefit to the domestic shipper. For instance, the shipper in the Annapolis Valley who uses the Canadian National to send goods to Toronto finds that it costs him more to do that than it costs his competitor to ship from Hamburg, Germany to Toronto. That is a fact, Mr. Speaker. As my poor frustrated shipper says, "Mr. member, we are supposed to be the wharf for the Atlan-

tic." We are told that we are lucky to live by the sea, smell the fresh air and watch Johnathon Livingstone Seagull go up and down and philosophize about his rhapsody as he soars down to try to catch a fish. Yes, it is a great place to live, but when it comes to hard economic facts there is geographic discrimination; we are far from the markets of the world and of central Canada. We understand that and we like to live there, but we cannot understand why the discrimination of geographic distance has to be compounded by the rate structure of the national railway system. It is strange that a Hamburg shipper can land his goods in Toronto cheaper than a producer in Atlantic Canada. We have the largest wharf in the world, Mr. Speaker; it stretches from Toronto to Halifax.
I will give another illustration of why we are frustrated with this system of transportation, and why members take the opportunity during the debate on the CN financing bill to try to point out that something has to be done. Let us talk about rates and not just the anomaly of Hamburg versus the Annapolis Valley. You can turn that around. My shipper cannot ship cheaper from the Annapolis Valley to Hamburg than the shipper in Toronto. I can prove that point by bills of lading.
I should like to read from the newsletter put out by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, a non-government agency of interested businessmen and, boards of trade with support from the four Atlantic provinces which deals with Atlantic problems. I do not think I could do it justice by paraphrasing, so I will read it as I want to give a little more detail than that of the Annapolis Valley-Hamburg situation to show what confronts us in Atlantic Canada when we talk about rates.
I might say that we are glad that at least the west had a conference about transportation. We are as convinced as they that provincial governments will finally have to look at the cost structure of railway operations. During the debates on the transportation bill in this House, many members spoke of the problems the bill was going to create unless we could see what the variable costs were. What does the railway charge against fixed or variable costs? This type of information is difficult for members of parliament or provincial governments to obtain, but I believe that in future provincial governments will be able to get some insight into the costing structure of the railways on a confidential basis. Of course, the CTC is going to study freight rate anomalies which prejudice the west; perhaps it could also study the freight rate anomalies that prejudice us in the east.
I should like to read from the APEC newsletter of August, 1973, which, among other things, says this:
As an example of the lack of alternatives and competition in the Atlantic region, due to the lack of volume there is no pool car service for less-than-car load traffic from Halifax to central Canada. But daily pool cars operate from Toronto to the Maritimes.
We are small down there. We cannot get the railways to get together to collect small shipments from small shippers into a pool car so that we can get a preferred charge for sending goods to central Canada. Every day pool cars come to the east under preferred charges, because the volume of traffic that can be picked up from central Canada warrants that arrangement. So, we cannot get pool
October 26, 1973

cars going west, but they do come east, and we must compete in that situation.
I do not blame this government for this state of affairs. All governments are to blame. Let me say that there is much talk about alienation, dissatisfaction and frustration in my part of Canada. Do not think that we, who come from the east, the cradle of this land, are all that happy about our transportation system. I well remember, when I was just knee-high to a grasshopper, that two places close to my home-and this was not Quebec-used to raise the black flag on July 1. I am not speaking of 1867, 1907 or 1927. I am talking about 1947 and 1957. The black flag ran up because some people thought that their prosperity had gone when we entered confederation. They have reason to wonder. I continue quoting:
The pool car alternative would introduce additional and desirable competition. Government should therefore consider partial sponsorship for the initial operation of a consolidation warehouse-
Could not the railways or the government consider establishing consolidation warehouses, so that we could have the benefit of the sort of pool car service that is available to central Canada for shipments to eastern Canada? I continue quoting:
-and regular pool car service from the Atlantic region to Central Canada.
Other anomalies and problems abound in the Atlantic region. In Eastern Canada the railways are capable of profitably shipping a minimum of twenty 20-foot containers a week, in any one direction, carrying exports or imports between Halifax and Toronto for $207 each. For a minimum annual contract of 18,000 export and import containers shipped between Central Canada and the Mari-times the rate falls to $132 each.
Let me make clear those figures. If you do not handle any great volume of containers, you will pay $207 for each one, but if you are a large conglomerate, or tied in with the trans-Atlantic shippers, or with CN at Halifax, you are going to pay only $132 for the same container. 1 continue quoting:
Present volume rates for import-export containers cover variable costs and make a net contribution to railway fixed costs; otherwise there would be no point in the railways offering special rates designed to attract container traffic carrying exports or imports which might otherwise be shipped through Montreal, the Seaway or an American port. In any case, as CTC President E. J. Benson stated on July 19:
'Section 23 of the National Transportation Act refers to Section 276, 277 and 278 of the Railway Act, and those sections require that the fixing of freight rates have regard to minimum and maximum levels:
(a)	No rate can be below the compensatory level-it must exceed the variable cost of the movement of the traffic concerned as determined by the Commission; and
(b)	A captive shipper who qualifies for a fixed rate is entitled to a rate which does not exceed variable cost by more than one hundred and fifty per cent.'
Thus it becomes difficult to understand why it costs $335 to send a domestically originated 20-foot container carrying only one-quarter of its maximum load, when it costs only $132 to send a comparable import container, carrying the maximum load, from Halifax to Toronto. It is even more difficult to accept a charge of $1,340 for a maximum load domestic container. That is a rate ten times as high as the minimum import container rate-import containers average about three-quarters of maximum load-despite the assistance received by the railway under the Maritimes Freight Rates Act.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
For a fully loaded 20-foot container carrying 40,000 lbs. of
domestic dry goods, the rail charge may rise to $1,656. This
exceeds the minimum rate for a comparable loaded export container by 1,155 per cent.
I know that when you quote figures you can become completely bulldozed, so to speak, and lose the attention of the audience. But we are not speaking for the audience; we are speaking for the record, in the hope that some of those who read these debates will wonder, as we wonder, why the east cannot compete with central Canada. We are far removed from the markets of central Canada and our container volume is not high. Our containers start their journey in Halifax, Annapolis Valley, Pictou and other regions. The rates given to our shippers are higher than the preferred export rates given to larger shippers who ship in large volume.
That brings me to my second point. I can understand that the railways will give preferential treatment to exporters who may export something like 18,000 containers per year. Obviously, the greater your volume is, the better is the rate you can command. Once that volume of traffic has been established flowing east and west, once you have containers going from Halifax to Toronto, why could you not give the Atlantic shipper a rate that is not the same, perhaps, but very close to that given to the importer or shipper who ships in large volume? That is the question we are asking, and we want some answers. The volume of traffic is there; large shippers are given preferred rates, but domestic shippers are discriminated against. That is not fair. Certainly, in view of the volume of traffic that the railways handle, there should be no discrimination against domestic shippers. They ought not to be discriminated against by an unreasonable rate.
On or about October 11, there was a transportation seminar in the Maritimes, when the Roads and Transportation Association of Canada met in Halifax. An interesting speech was made at that association meeting by a fellow called Robert Manuge who is executive vice-president and general manager of Anil Canada Ltd. of East River. He said, among other things:
The facts indicated that the railways may be deliberately discouraging the use of containers by domestic shippers in order to bolster box car traffic and rail revenues and prevent the circumvention of high commodity rail rates by captive Atlantic region rail shippers, ...
He went on to say:
It costs Anil, for example, $468 to send 40,000 pounds of its products from Nova Scotia to Toronto by rail. It costs $132 to send a comparable import container, carrying the maximum load, from Halifax to Toronto.
'Why must a local firm accept a charge that is 164 per cent to 255 per cent higher than the rate available to imported containers, perhaps carrying the same products from an overseas competitor, despite the assistance under the Maritime Freight Rates Act?'...
Earlier, he had said that the east coast is really the gateway to Canada. I suggest that we are just a pipeline. Goods are piped from Halifax to Toronto and, under present rate structures, the benefit does not accrue to us.
The next question is this. Why should we continue the present rate structure which encourages the development of the inner core of the country and the development of secondary industries which do the processing and develop-

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
ing in central Canada. Again, with a little imagination, effort-

-and common sense, it should be possible to help the Maritimes in this regard. We do not want big cities like Toronto springing up on the east coast; on the other hand, we would not mind a few little Oakvilles, Port Credits or similar areas. We do not want the megalopolises and metropolises which are causing so many problems in other parts of Canada. I do not want to overstress that. I know other hon. members want to speak and will limit my remarks.
The point is that the federal government should consider a transportation policy of the kind that was envisaged in 1867 when all parts of the country were considered equal. That is how they should be now. Transportation policy is a tool for national economic development of the regions. If the regions are strong, the whole country will be strong. This applies to apples, to life, and to transportation.
Further, the system should be changed so that it is more efficient than the one we have now. Now, we take the taxpayers' money to subsidize inefficiency.
My third point is that the domestic shipper should not be discriminated against merely because he does not send out the volume of container traffic that the importer or exporter sends. He should be given a fair rate, so that he can compete with that type of shipper. There are many other areas one could mention and about which one could ask questions. When talking about efficiency, why does it take 35 hours for the so-called unit train out of Halifax to reach Montreal? It is only 780 miles, so that must be one of the slowest rates of progress anywhere in Canada.

speechtext:
Air Canada service is definitely much better than when I first came to this House. It used to take between six and eight hours to travel from Ottawa to Halifax. You had to transfer in Montreal and there was a wait of from two to four hours. Fortunately, there is now one plane a day that flies directly to Halifax from Ottawa. It takes one and a quarter hours or one hour and 20 minutes. My point is, how can there be competition between different modes of transportation that are owned by the same company. Nevertheless, we still work under this mythology of compensatory rates when it helps others, but forget about it when it hurts us.
I know there are other members who want to speak on this bill. I just want to mention that the railways are as much a part of this country as the tides in the Bay of Fundy. Those tides are the highest in the world. We on the shores of the Bay of Fundy wonder which will change first, the tides that flow in and out or the transportation system. If we can be assured that when this bill is referred to the committee, officials of CNR, CPR and Air Canada will appear before the committee to give more detailed answers to some of the questions we have been asking, this might help the Minister of Transport in trying to work out some of the fundamental problems of this country.
We talk about regional disparity, the problems of bilingualism and the sincere efforts of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to develop those areas in Canada which do not receive the benefits of other areas. However, I say in all seriousness there will never be an effective policy of regional economic expansion in the hinterland and periphery of this country until we have a transportation system that will develop in a more meaningful way the very areas that DREE is supposed to help. I can give examples of this in my own constituency. Companies are receiving DREE grants to cover customers west of the Lakehead. Because of the successive freight rate increases in the past two or three years, they received DREE grants to expand their facilities to serve the market west of the Lakehead. However, because of the seven, eight or nine freight rate increases in the past year and a half or two years, they can hardly service the customers they have east of the Lakehead.
I plead with the Minister of Transport to accept what was requested by the western premiers. I know the Atlantic premiers would ask for the same. Frankly, any Canadian would ask that transportation be a fundamental tool of economic development, no matter where he lives. In this way, all Canadians would benefit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to use this opportunity to reiterate a plea I made ever since coming here. That is that the government of Canada, the Department of Transport and other agencies which deal with the various aspects of transportation should begin to look at the whole question of transportation needs in this country in its entirety rather than in separate compartments, as has been done over the years. It seems that at present the one objective of each agency and department is to not let the other know what it is doing. In no other country can that kind of attitude have such a detrimental effect as it does in Canada. There are 22 million people in this country who inhabit some three
October 26, 1973

million or four million square miles of land, yet we use our transportation facilities on the most illogical wasteful manner that can be imagined. I wish to give an illustration of what I mean.
When I was first elected to this House 12 years ago, there were six or seven trains a day between Ottawa and Montreal, and the same number between Montreal and Ottawa. They departed at various times during the day. They moved quickly and provided an easy and comfortable method of travelling between Ottawa and Montreal and return. What has been done? We, the government of Canada-

speechtext:
We, the parliament of Canada, allowed the railways, with the blessings of the Canadian Transport Commission and before that the Board of Transport Commissioners, to cut back on the number of trains per day and the meal service. We allowed them to change the times to the point where it now seems they do not want people to travel on their trains. What we found, of course, was that more people used their cars. There was an expansion of bus service-buses left every hour on the hour. What could be more stupid at a time when we are concerned about the fuel shortage and the befouling of the environment than to cut back on railways which can carry people in large numbers quickly and relatively cheaply?
But that was not enough. Though we apparently have no money to subsidize rail transport from Ottawa to Montreal, another branch of the government is proposing to invest $200 million or $300 million in a STOL aircraft system which instead of taking two hours from downtown Ottawa as the train does to downtown Montreal will take half an hour by air, but passengers will have to spend half an hour getting to the airport and another half an hour getting from the airport at the other end to downtown Montreal.

speechtext:
That is just one instance of the failure of the government, and of the Department of Transport in particular, to provide the kind of overall efficient service which the people need.
I want to talk for a few minutes about Air Canada and the CN. I do not think I need explain to members of parliament that I am a supporter of Air Canada and of the principle that air transport should be operated mainly, if not exclusively, by a publicly-owned corporation or under its jurisdiction. If I express criticism of Air Canada, as I intend to do, I do so with a great deal of regret; I wish I could spend my time complimenting Air Canada on the work it is doing. It did a magnificent job for many years. The decline began during the period when a Conservative government was in power, and the so-called regional carriers were given the short runs while Canadian Pacific was permitted and encouraged to get into the trans-Canadian and international air transport business in competition with Air Canada. Air Canada is not performing well at the present time.
