speechtext:
The relationship between the company and its employees is poor. The morale of the employees at all levels is bad. Air Canada's relationship with its customers leaves a great deal to be desired. I want to document what I say because I think the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has the responsibility to take whatever steps may be necessary to change this situation. I intend to put forward one or two suggestions as to ways in which this ought to be done.
A few years ago, Air Canada, or Air Canada in consultation with the government, arranged for a study of its organization to be carried out in depth. This study was undertaken by a United States company-why a United States company was chosen, I do not know. But as a result of that study, and the recommendations forthcoming from it, a large number of changes were made in senior personnel. Many of the senior staff from Vice-Presidents down were retired. I know that many of them really did not want to retire. New people were brought in to take over their jobs. The number of vice-presidents was increased; today, I understand, there are some 19 vice-presidents.
I can see no improvement, Mr. Speaker, as a result of the wholesale changes which were made. It is fairly obvious there is a great deal of discontent among those who have remained and evidence of this is the fact that Mr. Baldwin, who was the number two man in Air Canada, has announced his retirement before reaching the retirement age. Then again, there have been a whole series of disputes between the management of Air Canada and its employees. There was the strike of machinists which tied up operations completely some time ago and, more recently, there was a strike of employees working in the finance department in Winnipeg.
The issues which led to the strike, and which made it necessary for the employees to withdraw their labour for a long period, were not particularly difficult to solve had there been understanding and goodwill on the part of management. The employees were afraid that following the development of a computer centre in Montreal the work they were doing in Winnipeg would be transferred to Montreal. They were afraid they would be obliged to move to Montreal if they wished to keep their jobs. It is true that the management of Air Canada assured them this would not happen. But we in Manitoba, regardless of whether we live in Winnipeg or in rural areas, regardless of whether we are members of a chamber of commerce or of a labour union, and regardless of the political party to which we may belong, cannot help but remember what happened a number of years ago when, despite denials by Air Canada management that the overhaul base in Winnipeg would be, first cut back, and then eliminated altogether and moved to Montreal, such a move did, in fact, take place. The overhaul base in Winnipeg, which at one time employed 2,000 workers is now a thing of the past and all that work is being done in Montreal, despite denials by the company, denials persisting for years, that such a step would be taken. It is not surprising, in these circumstances, that the workers to whom I have referred, along with others, are suspicious of Air Canada management, and this atmosphere of suspicion does not lend itself
7274

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
to efficient work and the provision of satisfactory service to customers.
As one who travels frequently on Air Canada I want to say that I consider the food which is served to passengers to be, on occasion, of a very inferior nature. In fact, on occasion it is a disaster. I have discussed this matter both publicly and privately with representatives of Air Canada with absolutely no success. When I raise the matter I am told I am the only person who does so. But when I asked certain questions in parliament about that aspect of the matter, the answer I received was framed in such a way that it was virtually impossible to know how many people had complained. I am sure I did not get this indirect, roundabout answer by accident. I am sure they did not want to tell me how frequently complaints are made. I wonder how much monitoring of the quality of the food provided is carried out by Air Canada personnel. I wonder whether Air Canada has looked into the advisability of preparing its own meals. I am told that CP Air prepares its own meals. I do not like giving a private carrier credit, but on the few occasions I have travelled CP Air I found the food superior to that served by Air Canada.
I should like to give a third illustration-and these illustrations come to mind without my doing an in-depth study of Air Canada. Let me talk about timetabling. Ordinarily, I go to Winnipeg on Friday, leaving Ottawa at five o'clock. During the supper hour, which I suppose is a period lasting about an hour and a half, the situation at the Winnipeg airport is such that the following Air Canada planes arrive. There is one 1011 which has a capacity of about 300 passengers; there is one DC-8 stretched which has a capacity of about 200 passengers; there are two DC-9's each with a capacity of about 100 passengers. At this time of year those planes are travelling almost at capacity, if they are not overbooked. At the same time one plane arrives in Winnipeg from the United States, a Northwest Airlines plane, and so does one CP Air plane.
Air Canada says that this is not their responsibility, that they did not build the airport facilities. However, they are responsible for their own timetabling. They could stretch their air arrivals at this time so that four aircraft did not arrive at virtually the same time. At the present time you wait for your Air Canada baggage for up to an hour or more at this particular period of the day. I wish the Minister of Transport would go to Winnipeg and examine this situation, because it means there are literally hundreds of cars which have to park in areas where no parking is allowed. You cannot blame people who come to meet their friends or relatives, because there just is no other place to park; parking areas are fully occupied. Then when someone gets a ticket and pays a fine for over-parking because the person he met had to wait for his baggage, his thoughts about Air Canada are not very complimentary.
Let me now mention a situation which does not affect me personally all that much since I am one of those fortunate people who fly from Ottawa to Winnipeg direct, which accounts for about 95 per cent of the flights that I make during the course of a year. I do not have to travel via Toronto, but if there ever was a monstrosity which

seems to be have been designed with the express purpose of making things difficult, uncomfortable and unpleasant for passengers, it is terminal 2 in Toronto. I realize this is not Air Canada's fault either. I know this because on one occasion when I did have to spend a little time at Toronto airport I wrote to Mr. Baldwin, and he told me the truth in his reply that it was not Air Canada's fault. The Department of Transport had designed terminal 2 and had it constructed. But, as I say, if there ever was a monstrosity, an abortion, a total disaster area, it is that terminal.

speechtext:
It is speculation, but whoever was responsible should certainly have his head examined by a psychiatrist. One has to walk miles at terminal two. In the Montreal Star for yesterday or the day before, I noticed a short letter, which I should have clipped and read to the House today, written by someone who was reporting that his sister needed a wheelchair when she arrived at the Toronto airport. However, even though notification had been given in advance, no wheelchair was waiting and she had to walk miles on her crutches to get from where she deplaned to the taxi or bus. I hear there are motorized carts, but the number of times I have seen passengers riding from one part of the terminal to another are few and far between. There are no comfortable chairs or couches on which to sit if one has to wait. I could go on and on, but I am sure hon. members who use Toronto airport more frequently than I can wax much more eloquent about the terminal's shortcomings.
I should like to give another illustration before leaving the Toronto airport terminal. The department seems to feel that the present situation is not bad enough and it is going to extend the terminal, doubling its size so people have to walk five miles instead of two. I suggest that the minister make sure that his department knows what it is doing and uses some common sense before he permits any extension of that facility.
Let me make one further personal observation. Several years ago, supposedly because it was more efficient and would save money to do so, the reservations office in the Ottawa area, which used to be reached by dialing the phone and speaking to someone in Ottawa, was moved to Montreal. I am not criticizing Montreal for this; we were told it would be more efficient to make this move. Last Thursday, at about 11.30 in the evening, I wanted to check whether the flight I was taking on Friday morning had in fact been confirmed. I dialed the reservations number for Air Canada repeatedly for two hours, and each time my call was answered I heard a recording which told me that the lines were busy and I should hold. I held the line on a number of occasions for up to ten minutes but no one came on the line to answer my call. Eventually I gave up. Fortunately for me the next morning I was able to confirm my flight and I was able to travel. This kind of service is
October 26, 1973

intolerable and inexcusable. If this is what efficiency means, then I think Air Canada should return to its old system which it said was less efficient. It was probably a little more costly, but at least you could find out whether or not you would get a seat.
One last word about air travel. I suppose I shall be told this is not Air Canada's fault either but the fault of the Department of Transport. People in Winnipeg and Manitoba have been making a case for a number of years that they are entitled to a Canadian route from Winnipeg to Minneapolis and Chicago. At present we are served by only one carrier, a United States carrier, Northwest Airlines. This carrier has a record of poor relationships with its employees. Several strikes have shut down its operations over the past number of years, strikes lasting, in one case at least, for substantially more than one month. So in fact there was no direct service from Winnipeg to the midwestern United States. Winnipeg has been pleading for a Canadian line and I should have hoped it would be operated by Air Canada, but I would settle for one of the other airlines.
A few weeks ago the minister announced they were close to an agreement after long negotiation with representatives of the United States on the extension of air routes to the United States by Canadian carriers and to Canada by United States carriers. The minister announced there would be 18 new routes for Canadian carriers. That announcement was welcomed by all Canadians. Let me tell the minister that western Canadians, Manitobans in particular, were unhappy, to say the least, to find out that the agreement negotiated on behalf of all Canadians did not provide for a direct Canadian route from Manitoba to the midwestern United States until at least 1978. If I were to use the language I have heard about this, Mr. Speaker, you would immediately suggest that I was using unparliamentary language.
This means we will have to wait five more years before we have a direct Canadian route. This is the kind of treatment western Canadians have been receiving for generations. This is the kind of treatment that has led to the alienation, which is increasing, I am sorry to say, in western Canada and the kind of treatment that leads to a situation in which the Liberal Party has been almost eliminated in terms of members of parliament from the three prairie provinces. Let me say to the Minister of Transport and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that if they wish to change what has happened during recent elections in western Canada, they should take another look at the kind of treatment they have permitted-I do not use the word "encouraged"

to take place in western Canada.
I think I have said as much as I want to on this occasion about Air Canada and I hope some of the people who have responsibility in this airline will pay attention to my criticisms. I do not want to be only critical of Air Canada, because criticism alone does not help to improve conditions which have led to the kind of problems I have illustrated. Let me say to the Minister of Transport and to the government that the situation which has developed in respect of Air Canada will continue at least until the government does several things.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
First of all, the government ought to take a very hard look at the membership of the board of directors who supposedly run Air Canada. The situation in respect of Air Canada is so serious that the time has long passed when people should be appointed to the board of directors simply because they belong to the right political party or because they come from a geographic area that should have representation. If Air Canada is to be drastically changed, as I believe I have illustrated it must be changed, it needs a new, vigorous and competent board of directors. I would not presume to suggest who should replace those now on the board but I urge the minister to completely change the composition of the present board.
Second, I suggest to the minister that the performance of the senior management of Air Canada must be examined thoroughly. I do not believe they are doing the job that ought to be done, and a great deal needs to be done. I think the illustrations I have given of the incompetence of Air Canada bear that out. I was not the greatest admirer of Mr. Baldwin when he was deputy minister of transport, but when I read that he was retiring several years early I could not help asking myself-I hope the minister will give this some thought-whether in fact the wrong man was retiring. To put it mildly, I would say I am disillusioned with the job being done by Mr. Pratte, president of Air Canada, and the kind of people who have been appointed, I presume on his recommendation, as vice-presidents.
I urge the minister to give serious consideration to the kind of people leading Air Canada, particularly those in the upper echelons. Until the employees of Air Canada have the feeling that the company is operating efficiently and in a way which gives them fair treatment, and that the company cares about what is happening to its customers and its services, nothing will improve.
Let me say one more thing about terminal 2 to demonstrate that what I have suggested is not exaggerated. The management of Air Canada arranged for a survey of customer services and customer feelings about Air Canada particularly in relation to the proposed movement to the new terminal in Toronto. That survey was carried out by a Miss Farnen. I will not take the time to put on the record what she said, although I can and will do so probably at a future meeting of the transport committee. A more damning indictment of Air Canada and its operations could not be found.
As things now exist, it is as though that report prepared at the request of Air Canada management was never made. The report has disappeared, and as far as I can tell very few employees at the senior, middle or lower levels of Air Canada have ever seen it. From my reading of the report and its recommendations, it would seem that virtually none of the problems have been corrected and none of the recommendations have been implemented. I suggest that not all of the recommendations would be difficult to implement and many would not have cost much money. One recommendation in the report was for the employment of more staff. This recommendation was ignored until the management of Air Canada saw how bad the situation was and decided a move had to be made. This is being carried out to at least a partial degree. I would urge
26635-30 J

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada the minister to take a serious look at the operations of Air Canada.
Let me say a few words about the entire operations of our railways. I do not fault the CNR exclusively, although I do fault what seems to be the attitude of CNR management. That attitude seems to be that the CN can only do those things the CPR is prepared to do. It seems they feel they cannot compete with the CPR in order to give cheaper, better and faster service, but that they should do everything possible along with the CPR to provide worse service than was provided before.
I give a small illustration of what I mean. If a person in Ottawa wished to take a train to Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg or somewhere else and wanted to know the time of arrival or departure of a train, he would pick up the Ottawa telephone book and look under the listing for CPR or CNR. Until a year or two ago the first number listed under the CPR or the CNR heading was "train information." Now one would have to have a better pair of glasses than I have in order to look down the page about a column and a half in order to find the "train information" listing.
In my view, this has not occurred as a result of an accident; I suggest it is a deliberate attempt to discourage people asking questions and indeed to travel as passengers on either railway. This has been done jointly, rather than separately. I could not begin to make the case for improvements in rail service as a whole and particularly for improvements in rail service in respect of freight as well as was done by the four western premiers at the Western Economic Opportunities conference in July of this year. I think it is significant that the proposals on what should be done, and the criticism of existing practices that was made at that conference were made by the four premiers, three of whom lead NDP governments and the fourth of whom is the Conservative Premier of Alberta.
It was interesting and important to me as a westerner to read the report which appeared in all the newspapers. They all reported the same fact, to the effect that the spokesman on the question of transportation for the four premiers was the Conservative Premier of Alberta. It is not my intention to place on the record everything they said, but what they said was so convincing that I am certain no one in western Canada, regardless of political affiliation or social or economic background-and, indeed, no fair-minded thinking person in central Canada or in the maritime provinces-could disagree, because they said essentially that the railway systems of this country were established primarily because without them there would have been no country.
They were established at a time when the manufactured goods which were being produced or processed in central Canada had to be shipped to the Maritimes and to western Canada, and the raw materials, the products of our forests, the minerals, the fish and everything else which was produced in western Canada and in the maritime provinces, had to be moved by rail to central Canada. The whole system of freight rates was established with that in mind.
One hundred years have now gone by. Situations have changed, and now we have resources in the prairie prov-

inces, in British Columbia and in the maritime provinces which can be processed and manufactured as cheaply and as efficiently near the source of growth, near the source from which they are brought out of the ground, as they can in central Canada. This was not the case until now, to large extent because the whole system of freight rates is designed to guarantee the situation we had in the first 75 years of the history of this country.
The people of western Canada and the maritime provinces are not content to let that situation continue. They are not content to see the job-creating manufacturing industries, to a large extent because of discriminatory freight rates, be expanded in central Canada so that people from the Maritimes, the Prairies and British Columbia are virtually forced to move to Ontario or to the Montreal area of Quebec. They want, and are entitled to have, their fair share. We are not asking that the manufacturing industries or the processing of our minerals, our forests or our fisheries, be carried out in our own areas regardless of cost. We are asking, as indeed the prairie premiers were demanding on behalf of the people of their regions, that the discrimination which has existed should be eliminated and that a new system of transportation with a new system of calculating freight rates be established.
I shall give a few illustrations of the type of discrimination which exists. My colleague, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) listed some of them in an article he wrote in the Toronto Globe and Mail. I could do the same thing by quoting from the briefs which the prairie premiers presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at that conference. It costs $2.90 a hundredweight to ship livestock from Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, to Toronto. If the livestock were slaughtered and dressed in Prince Albert, thus providing jobs to the people of Saskatchewan, it would cost $3.37 a hundredweight to ship the meat to Toronto.
Unprocessed rapeseed shipped from Saskatchewan to Vancouver costs 35 cents per 100 pounds, but if it were processed into oil before shipment it would cost $1.21 per 100 pounds to ship it from Saskatchewan to Vancouver. It costs $38 to ship a ton of Manitoba nickel to eastern factories, but $138 a ton to ship the product of the processed nickel from eastern factories back to Manitoba. It costs $2.01 per 100 pounds to ship a 60,000 pound minimum carload of canned foodstuff from Portage la Prairie, Manitoba, to Vancouver, while the rate to ship the same item from Toronto to Vancouver is $2.08; yet the distance from Toronto to Vancouver is about twice that from Portage la Prairie to Vancouver. Why does this type of situation develop?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say, first of all, that I shall be as brief as possible. I recognize that many members wish to speak in this important debate. First I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for once again having raised in this chamber a matter which I think is of very great importance, the pension question in respect of retired railway workers. Of course, this is not the first time the matter has been raised, but I think it is time it was raised again and I am grateful to my hon. friend for having raised it in the debate earlier today.
During the unhappy debate on the "back to work" bill of nearly two months ago, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, myself and the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) touched on this problem. Since that time, despite the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) suggested that some action would be taken to study the situation of the railway pensioners, nothing has happened. I am not directing my remarks especially to colleagues on the government side but to other members in the chamber and I ask them to use what influence they have to approach the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and encourage them to bring about a study of railway pensions, especially those of retired railway workers.
I would remind hon. members that when this matter came up-it is reported in Hansard of August 31, 1973, at page 6135-I put the following question to the Minister of Labour:
So my question to the minister is, can he give us some assurance that this whole question will be gone into? If the minister does not want to go that far at this time, can he give us the assurance that he will meet as soon as possible, which means almost immediately-and I recognize the demands on his time at the moment-with representatives of this pension group so that immediate negotiations can take place with a view to setting up an inquiry to send once and for all this running sore . . .
The Minister of Labour replied as follows and I ask members on the government side to pay attention to these words:
Yes, with reference to those already retired. I think this is quite a legitimate position, but I do not think it can be accomplished relative to the bill before us today.
He was referring to the fact that he had announced the appointment of Mr. John Deutsch to look into certain aspects of the pension plan. Myself and other hon. members whom I mentioned wanted him to appoint a committee to look into all aspects of the pension plan, especially from the point of view of retired railway workers. The minister said that there were certain options, as follows:
There is the question of whether it could be done through a joint committee, something similar to what was done before with assistance from governmental officials, if you like, from my department and the Department of Transport.
He then went on:
. . . perhaps an industrial commissioner should look into the whole broad question. So, as I assured the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I am now assuring the hon. member for Vancouver South that I would be prepared, as would the Minister of Transport, to bring the parties together to see what further significant changes can be made to improve these pensions.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
This is the commitment from the government. That is why I again ask government members to remember that this commitment has been made, and in the next few days to take the time and trouble to speak to their ministers, because I know the concern for retired railway workers is not confined to one side of the House. I know there are hon. members on the government side, as there are in the Social Credit party and in the NDP, as well as in my own party, who are equally concerned. This is part of the whole problem within the railways. The hon. member for Sas-katoon-Biggar pointed out the following in the debate a month and a half ago:
If the minister or this government think that they can divorce the matter of pensions from the over-all settlement of this rail dispute, then let me tell them that they are wrong.
I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar in that statement and I ask hon. members to remember that the problems which lie within the railway trades at the moment will not go away. There is every expectation that they will be recurring, and I say to all hon. members that the question of pensions is one of them. The matter was raised again on September 14, 1973, as recorded at page 6597 of Hansard, again by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he asked the Minister of Labour what was being done about the commitment he had given. The Minister of Labour replied:
I did say that a supplemental study of the benefit structure of the pensions as opposed to the costing was under consideration, and I advise the hon. member that it is still under consideration. Discussions will have to be held with the railways concerned, the Minister of Transport and the union leadership, and we will get these discussions under way as soon as we can.
That is all very well, but again I ask hon. members to take note that these discussions must take place. It is not enough to tell us that the matter is continually under study. In the minister's remarks, may I point out with respect, there is a very important omission, that is, there was indication that the minister or his officials would speak to the Association of Railway Pensioners of Canada which, as some hon. members know, numbers some 20,000 people. These people have their own organization and they must be brought into these discussions. I point out to government members, to the Minister of Labour and to the Minister of Transport, that the commitment is there and we expect them to fulfil it. We say earnestly and sincerely that this is a serious matter and should not be left too long.
I want to mention another matter, that is, the continuing serious difficulty regarding the morale of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers in my own city. During the committee stage of this bill I asked that the representatives of these workmen be brought before the standing committee to explain to hon. members just what is the problem as they see it, because once again this problem will not go away and it ill behooves us to pretend that this is just a union dispute or just a disagreement between some of the workers and the companies.
This is a matter that is striking right at the heart of the efficiency of the transportation system of Canada, and in the process is causing a great deal of hardship and anguish to the railwaymen involved. I say, and it is important that it be remembered, that we are not dealing here with a group of people who are in any way irresponsible. I have

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the bill before us today I should like to touch upon what I feel is the unfortunate failure of the CNR and the government to supply commuter service in our urban centres. My area of York-Simcoe is particularly hard hit by this neglect. For many years residents have asked for the re-establishment of the passenger service that once existed between the Aurora-Newmarket area and Toronto. The present lack of such a service is due, in the main, to unfortunate jurisdictional confusion and indifference on the part of many, including this government. In my opinion, this neglect must end.
It was not enough for this Liberal government simply to provide an experimental train that commenced to run in my riding on November 1, only two or three days after the last election, but which was discontinued eight weeks later. A commuter train service is urgently needed by the residents of York-Simcoe which has grown greatly in the past 12 years. In 1961 the riding had a population of 72,000; in 1971 it was 99,000 people, and today it is estimated to be over 102,000. In April last year I surveyed the residents and found that 94 per cent wished to have a commuter service. Of the number answering the inquiry, many indicated that they would use the service if it were available.
The GO transit Gray Coach service between Newmarket and Toronto has been well received and is now running at near break-even point. I understand from the GO transit officials that a commuter train would be complementary rather than compete with the present GO transit system. It was the original intention of the province of Ontario that the service be an integrated one between the railroad and the bus line, namely, Gray Coach. Unfortunately, when the province of Ontario attempted to negotiate a satisfactory running contract with the CNR they were

unable to do so because of the high costing methods instituted by the CNR with respect to this line.
I would suggest that accounting procedures and conflicting philosophies add to the confusion when attempts are made to cost-out a commuter train service in Canada, and certainly in my riding. For example, in the 1971 annual report of the CNR it is stated that CN policy is as follows:
to make the provision of passenger services as far as possible a paying proposition for the railway within the framework of the National Transportation Act of 1967.
As part of that policy the company is pursuing vigorously all the advantages available to it under sections of the act which provide that passenger services uneconomic to the railways but needed by the public may receive federal government subsidies of up to 80 per cent of the losses on such services. Accordingly, during 1971 CN submitted to the Canadian Transport Commission applications for discontinuance of all intercity railway passenger services including its transcontinental service. This move was dictated by a provision in the act which stipulated that a railway must apply for discontinuance in order to qualify for subsidy payments.
Legislation provides for different procedures in the case of commuter service. In accordance with these procedures the company also applied to the commission to have the actual losses declared for its Montreal commuting services and for a recommendation to the governor in council for assistance in respect of such losses.
I found that statement most interesting, Mr. Speaker. Although the CNR and the government have denied that the government has covered deficits in connection with urban commuter services across Canada, for some time it has been suspected that the commuter train service in Montreal has been running at a deficit and that the federal government has been picking up that deficit directly or indirectly. In this connection I would draw the attention of the House to a statement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who is not in the House today to listen to the debate I am extremely disappointed about that. In answer to a written question which appears at page 5863 of Hansard for July 23, 1973, the minister said:
The management of Canadian National Railways advises CNR incurred a deficit of $2.1 million in 1970, $2.2 million in 1971 and estimates of a deficit of $2.4 million for 1972.
That refers to the operation of the Montreal commuter train service in those years. I think this is particularly significant, Mr. Speaker, because I can show to any member who is interested letters and representations indicating that the government in no way was picking up the deficit on the Montreal commuter service operated by CNR. Yet we have on record an admission by the minister that something like $2 million is being absorbed in losses by the CN to provide those services in Montreal, which in turn is a loss to the people of Canada.
Turning again to the annual report of the CNR, I would point out that the balance sheet as at December 31, 1972, reflects property investment of $3,476 billion after depreciation of $1,392 billion. Government of Canada loans are shown at over $1 billion and Canada's shareholder equity in Canadian National Railways was set at $2 billion. In that year the railways net interest paid on debt was $66 million which, by coincidence, was equal to the entire revenue received by the railway for their passenger services. In short, Mr. Speaker, the entire revenue that the CNR earned in that year from supplying passenger service
October 26, 1973

was diverted into an interest charge which was mainly a payment back to the government.
In addition, the road property was depreciated in the amount of $62.9 million, and the CN paid $62.7 million in various forms of taxes to various governments. These three items, totalling $191.6 million, represented over 15 per cent of Canadian National Railways total railway revenues in 1972. In reporting on the 1972 financial statements of the CN, the company's new auditors-I emphasize "new auditors"-pointed out that in January 1, 1923, all properties and equipment brought into the system at that date were included in the CN values and since that date all additions have been recorded at cost and depreciated thereafter. One wonders who is the net loser in this practice of so capitalizing, depreciating the items and in the meantime carrying interest-bearing debt mainly in the name of the federal government. Surely it works to the detriment of the persons who wish to use the railway as a public service.
Certainly if our highway system in Ontario were handled in a similar way, it would result in greatly higher annual costs which would have to be borne by the general taxpayers or by the users of our highways. In this connection it is interesting to note that on March 31, 1967, the province of Ontario wrote down to $1 approximately $3 billion worth of highways and thus ended the earlier practice of depreciating such highways on a 30-year basis. Since that write-off the province has spent almost $200 million per year for railway construction, but each year the amount is written off and paid out of general taxation in the province. In addition, the province has extended municipal grants for roadway construction totalling approximately $150 million a year, which again are written off each year. As a result, Ontario has a relatively good highway system which is used by motorists at relatively low cost.
It can be seen that the province could place a $4 billion value on our road system, which at 6 per cent would result in an annual charge to somebody of $240 million per year; and if the capitalized road system was depreciated on a 30-year basis it would require a further $130 million per year. Partly due to an historical quirk and partly due to different philosophies, our highway system has been structured to give the user a break while our railway system is structured to give the passenger an unduly heavy load.
I also wish to point out that, offsetting a low-cost road system, we have high-cost automobiles in this country. The financial cost to the average passenger car commuter is prohibitive. Take, as an example, my riding of York-Simcoe. The average person who commutes to Toronto has to travel 80 miles per day. It is generally accepted that a person's cost of driving an automobile is 12 cents per mile, or $9.60 per day. Assuming that there are IV2 passengers per motor car, it can be seen that the average commuter spends $6.40 per day travelling to and from work if he lives in my riding and works in downtown Toronto. Putting this another way, he would spend $30 per week, or $1,500 per year. That is what the commuter must spend. Before taxes, such a worker has to earn over $2,000 per year in order to pay his way by car to and from work.
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
It is often forgotten that any subsidy at the municipal, provincial or federal level which would assist the commuter to get to and from work at the lowest cost is really a saving, not a subsidy, for the general community. I emphasize that it is the federal government's wrong philosophy that has allowed the present situation to arise. Let me also stress that highways are dangerous; travelling on those highways in a motor vehicle is particularly dangerous. In the York region, 66 people were killed in highway traffic accidents in 1972, compared with 59 the year before. Every year the number of accidents on our highways increases.
Of course, the increasing volume of traffic merely highlights the congestion of our roads. Let me give some examples of what I mean, Mr. Speaker. Highway 400, for example, carried 67 per cent more people in 1972 then it carried in 1968. In 1972, the average daily traffic on that road was 34,900, compared with 23,476 in 1968. I point out, also, that pollution is a natural by-product of automobile usage. The report of the Ontario Advisory Committee on Energy, dated March, 1973, reads as follows;
.. . transportation accounts for over half of the man-made pollutants emitted to the air in metropolitan Toronto.
The report says, as well, that the automobile is "by far the largest contributor in this category." It goes on to say:
. . . the automobile is the main, man-made source of pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide, hydrocarbons and lead.
Dealing specifically with carbon monoxide, the report states:
In high-density population areas with a high concentration of motor cars, the burden of carbon monoxide in the air can be an increasingly serious hazard to health.
At page 62 of the same volume, the report states:
Public transit contributes on the average much less pollution per passenger mile than does the private automobile.
In addition, the report points out that transportation is probably one of the most serious social and aesthetic problems associated with land use. It says:
High concentrations of automobiles in large urban areas have resulted in the development of massive expressways which are exceedingly costly, use large amounts of land needed for housing and other purposes, departmentalize cities, increase congestion, and generally lower the quality of life in their immediate vicinity.
Again I say that the government has been completely negligent in this area.

I again point out that energy is not available in unlimited quantities in Canada or in the world. Certainly, it should not be squandered and unnecessarily used for commuter travel. In 1970, 17 per cent of the total energy consumed in Ontario was used in the transportation sector. As I said yesterday, 80 per cent of the energy used in Ontario has to be imported into the province. The

October 26, 1973
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada fuel consumption of motor vehicles accounted for about four-fifths of this energy consumption.
The transportation sector in Ontario utilized, in 1970, 394 trillion BTU's of energy. By 1990, if present trends continue, the transportation sector will utilize 1,100 trillion BTU's. The utilization of commuter train services would help to minimize this large consumption of nonrenewable resources. Already there is gasoline rationing in the United States. The authorities in that country are considering the imposition of a 50 mile per hour speed limit and other ways in which to conserve fuel. It is only prudent for Canadians to minimize the needless use of the automobile, especially when commuter train facilities are so readily available. We can use trackage and railway stock that is already available in this country.
Historically, the residents of my area have fought for passenger train service for over 120 years. In 1849, 1,100 residents petitioned the federal government as it was then constituted to incorporate a railroad company which would serve the area with passenger and freight facilities. As a result, the Toronto, Simcoe and Lake Huron Union Railroad Company was incorporated and subsequently financed through lottery tickets which were sold throughout the district.
On May 16, 1853, the first steam train in Canada West ran from Toronto to Aurora carrying passengers and freight. Today, the powers conferred in 1849 to build and operate this railway are vested in the CNR, a federal Crown corporation. Those in control of the operation have chosen, however, to discontinue the passenger service but to keep the line for freight service. CNR officials have stated they make money on freight but passengers are trouble. Commuters may be more trouble than freight, but I believe we have now gone full circle. Rail systems were needed when the country was being developed, to carry both people and freight. That is why the railways received their franchises. Today, railways are needed for the same two purposes but of the two, people must come first.

that, given the proper working relationship with the CNR, it will be more than willing to institute commuter train services in the Toronto area and other parts of Ontario where they are required. That co-operation has not been forthcoming up to the present time.
We want to know why the government sees fit to subsidize the Montreal area, with respect to commuter service, to the extent of over $2 million per year, but will not even meet with the appropriate Ontario authorities in order to try to arrive at a working relationship regarding the institution of a commuter' train service in Toronto. In this connection I would emphasize, as most members are probably aware, the GO transit service that the government of Ontario is now running in the Toronto area is completely paid for by the provincial government. They have a net running cost arrangement with the CNR where the CNR, in spite of their method of costing, is paid 100 per cent of what they say is the cost of running that service.
The province of Ontario is picking up any deficit between the revenues they are able to earn and the actual running cost charged by the CNR. Even at that, I think it is wise to note that most of that service is now running at a breakeven point as far as the province is concerned, and on average it is resulting in a net loss of about 40 cents per person per day. The province has acted, but not the federal government.
I suggest that if a rail commuter service were instituted in my area, it would be successful and any loss would be an accounting loss, not an actual loss on the service. Such a service would be cheaper for commuters. It would certainly be safer. Pollution from automobile usage would be lessened and energy would be conserved.
May I conclude by saying that I sincerely hope the government will give to my area in 1973, or certainly in 1974, a passenger train service and in so doing at least restore us to the position we had in 1853.

Mr. Speaker, I have only four or five minutes before private members' hour at four o'clock. I begin by saying that the CNR financing bill before us is important to all members of this House for many and various reasons. In a constituency such as mine it is very important because there is a large area of the city of Melville in which about 600 people work. It is also important in a constituency such as mine that is basically rural, because of the farming population and problems associated with rural Canada.
This debate provides members with an opportunity to talk about the problems of transportation and rural Canadian life. The transportation system is vital and central to most of us who come from the so-called hinterland areas of this country. All you have to do is look at the freight rate structure in places like the Prairies, most of Quebec outside the Montreal area, the Atlantic provinces, northern Ontario and other parts of northern Canada to know what I mean. The transportation system, the freight rate structure and the anomalies in it are a large part of the reason for the rapid shift of population from rural Canada to urban centres. This can easily be seen by looking at events in the provinces of Manitoba and Sas-

katchewan in the past few years. There is lack of development because of the freight rate structure, a structure which provides lower freight rates for shipping raw materials out of the Prairies than finished goods or products.
I will give only one example of this because I think it will demonstrate what I am talking about. In the city of Prince Albert, which the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) represents, it costs $2.90 per hundredweight to ship livestock to Toronto. If the livestock are slaughtered and processed, it costs $3.37 per hundredweight. That means only one thing: we are exporting jobs from Saskatchewan and other parts of rural Canada to places such as Toronto. The freight rate structure is organized in such a way that it is more profitable to do the processing in the golden horseshoe area of southern Ontario or in the city of Montreal. We must get rid of that type of system if we are to develop this country in an economically planned fashion where the younger citizens of rural Canada have job opportunities in their own locals. A transportation system is vital to that end.
The problem is not only freight rates. It is also the abandonment of rail lines which serve small areas of Saskatchewan. Plans are for the abandonment of about
3,000	miles of rail lines in my province by Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. What will happen when that is done? Many little villages and hamlets exist only because they are service centres for the farmers. They have grain elevators to which farmers deliver their grain. If they are abandoned, these small communities will lose one of their focal points and will have little reason for being. It will be more expensive for the farmer who will have to transport his grain a greater distance.
There is also the question of station agents. This, again, takes away from the service that is being provided to people in rural communities. It makes things more difficult and costly for them. When we talk about the transportation system we are talking about something that is absolutely fundamental to the way of life of a great many people whether they live in the Prairies, in Quebec, in eastern Canada or in the northern parts of this country.
I see it is four o'clock, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps I could call it four o'clock at this time and continue at a later date.

October 26, 1973
Income Tax Rebate
I am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss the famous motion I submitted last January and which has been on the order paper under number 38 since then.
Since the purpose of this motion is for the benefit of all Canadians who own single family houses, I obviously hope to have the support of all memebers, all the more so because we can discuss this motion while dealing first with its application concerning our country's resources.
On the material side, this country is obviously one of the wealthiest in the world.
And although our trade always favoured England and our natural resources were generally developped for the Americans, we are nevertheless citizens of a country where the standard of living is rather high. Our young country having been generously endowed by nature, they have not succeeded in exploiting us completely. However, exploiting was felt chiefly at the housing level and as a result our country is suffering from a lack of decent housing for poor and low income people.
Inquiries made by the government have shown that it was impossible for a couple earning under $8,000 a year to consider buying a house. On the other hand, the government introduces local initiatives programs under which the salary is $100 a week for three or four months. Among those earning only $7,000 to $8,000 a year, Mr. Speaker, it is needless to say there are many government employees at the Federal, provincial and municipal levels. There are more than just a few people with annual earnings from $5,000 to $6,000 and unfortunately that kind of money is also too often the wages of a great number of trade or industry employees.
In short, all those people are not earning an income that would enable them to make a down payment on a house with high mortgage payments, to pay insurance and municipal and school taxes. In spite of all the measures introduced by the government, one realizes that not only has the problem not been solved but the situation is getting worse every day. As a matter of fact, in 1969, a three-bedroom single family house cost about $18,000 in the Quebec City area. In 1970, the cost of the same house, in the same area, had gone up to $20,000 and this year a three-bedroom single family house, or a 1,000 square-foot house, goes for $23,000 while it seems that houses of that kind in the Toronto area would sell for about $28,000.
It is also obvious that those who purchase a house are faced with interest rates much higher than in 1970.
I remember that during the election campaign Liberal candidates made some commitments in this connection. And yet interest rates keep on increasing. Because municipal and school taxes have been raised we have reached the point where some government programs and mainly those of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are out of reach for most people. Some programs are even out of reach to the very people they were supposed to help.
The fact that family heads cannot afford a house even though they earn $6,000 or $7,000 a year is a tragedy. This is due to the fact that the down payment, monthly mortgage payments, maintenance costs, service costs and taxes never stop increasing.
As for those who qualify for loans from caisses populates and CMHC we know how much they must pay. For

instance, a $30,000 loan at 9 per cent, which is the current interest rate of the CMHC, means that monthly payments of $248 will be required for 25 years. Therefore, after those 25 years, the owner will have paid $74,520, namely $30,000 for the repayment of his loan and $44,520 in interest charges and this does not take into account the municipal and school taxes and service costs. As I said, this is in the case of people who qualify for the CMHC program which we know well or who applied to a caisse populaire.
Besides if we know what happens to those who qualify this does not apply to everyone. As a former carpenter I am always most interested in visiting housing projects in my constituency.
About two months ago, during one of those visits, I met a young couple who had requested their mortgage company to review their payments. They were paying $189 a month. After two and a half years of this, they had paid back only $112 of the capital, with the rest of the payments going for expenses, insurance and interests. Obviously, you cannot pay for a house in such a situation. While there may be many who cannot afford to become owners, I think that we should not forget the category of people which I have just mentioned.
The case of the young couple which I gave as an example a moment ago is not unique. Many owners who succeeded in obtaining financial means a few years ago now face serious problems. And these problems have become so difficult to solve that many people ask themselves: How long shall we be able to keep our house?
Middle income families, and even what were once considered well-off people, are affected. They find out that after they have bought a house, they will have to pay for it three times. They will have to pay for it once to the contractor and twice to the finance company.
This situation is really unacceptable and I think that as far as interest is concerned, the problem cannot be solved today. The government, however, must bring forward a program designed to improve living conditions of Canadians who own single family dwellings.
Among improvements that would have both essential and efficient results, there is the implementation of the motion before us, that I introduced early in this session. I suggest that this motion can easily be carried out and meets the wishes of all Canadians.
All the people who have access to Hansard have seen as well, I guess, that during the previous years, our party emphasized on many occasions in this chamber the importance and urgency of carrying out measures to relieve Canadian homeowners. When asking that municipal and school taxes be deductible for income tax purposes, I feel this is not a special favour but rather a sort of justice, since municipal and school taxes are already deductible in the case of "big wheels" or companies that own apartment bouses.
You will all recall, I think, a letter received early in September, that was directed to every member of Parliament by the Chairman of the Canadian School Trustees Association, Mr. Walter W. Robson. The latter referred to a meeting of the School Trustees Association of all the
October 26, 1973

provinces, that was held in Quebec City, in May 1973. The following resolution had then been passed:
"It is therefore agreed that the Canadians School Trustees Association file a petition with the Minister of Finance of the government of Canada and the ministers of Finance of all the provinces so that they take financial steps that will enable homeowners and tenants to deduct the amount of their school taxes from their taxable income."
The letter goes on to say that the resolution had been sent to the Minister of Finance in Ottawa (Mr. Turner) and that copies were being prepared to be sent to his provincial counterparts.
These school trustees from a great many Canadian communities, urban as well as rural, state that they are speaking on behalf of a majority of men and women who have responsibilities in respect of Canadian taxpayers.
Because hon. members of this House also have responsibilities in respect of taxpayers, those of the Social Credit Party of Canada are pleased to join with the school trustees to claim for all taxpayers the right to deduct from their individual income tax returns the amounts paid as school taxes to the various school boards.
The position of the Social Credit Party of Canada is that ownership of his home by the head of the family contributes to the development of individuals, the welfare of their families and the health of society. If the platform of the party, as far as housing is concerned, is widely publicized during election periods, it is also true that, between general elections, we continue to call for various means of action on the part of this government.
To improve the well-being of Canadians, we propose various means. First, the incentive for building single family dwellings by guaranteeing long term loans at an interest rate which should not exceed 3 per cent. Second, the abolition of impediments to building constituted by present taxes and especially by the sales tax of 12 per cent on building materials. Third, the owners of single family dwellings should also benefit from an income tax exemption on their mortgage interest payments as well as on municipal and school taxes; however, this exemption should not exceed $1,000 a year.
The program of our party in the area of housing reflects the needs of the Canadian people, which were expressed and proved publicly during Creditist conventions held each year in different parts of the country. The hon. members of our party having been elected without the election fund of big finance, it is easy for us to fulfill our role honestly and to be the spokesmen for our electors in order to claim in this House the measures which are urgently needed to safeguard the freedom of families and assure them utmost security in a rich country like ours.
Creditist members have always been ahead and we are pleased today to note that we are not the only ones who request efficient social measures. Several groups, several associations and intermediary bodies have exposed their views on this subject.
In Le Soleil of September 17, for example, we can read, and I quote:
The Saint-Jean-Baptiste Society (SSJB) of the Chaudiere area, in order to promote residential construction, invites all governments to favour income tax deduction of mortgage interest payincome Tax Rebate
ments on a new property for a period of three years and to grant a deduction of municipal and school taxes on a residential property.
That is what stands out in the main resolution passed by the membership of SSJB Chaudiere at the annual convention that was held last week in Ville Saint-Georges de Bauce under the chairmanship of Mr. Andre Breton . . .
People are generally aware of the benefits that would flow from the implementation of that motion to make property taxes deductible for tax purposes. Mr. Speaker, even Liberal supporters are in favour; all newspapers in the country mentioned that Liberal supporters gathered at the convention around mid-September in the federal capital passed a resolution asking that interest rates be reduced and even that amounts paid as interests on mortgage loans be made deductible for tax purposes.
Mr. Speaker, I earnestly hope that all members, Liberal members included, will have the courage to forget about bagmen for a moment and vote in favour of my motion.

speechtext:
I think I should continue. The question posed by motion No. 38 is whether or not it will truly benefit those citizens who must need such benefit. The motion provides, not for a tax deduction but for a tax credit which is applied against income tax owing by a citizen. If this concept were presented to the House as a bill it would permit an individual to deduct from his taxes owing an amount equal, apparently, to the combination of the interest payable on his mortgage in a given year and his municipal taxes payable in the same year.
I think it follows, very obviously, that to the extent that an individual pays more income taxes, to the extent that he pays more mortgage interest, to the extent that he pays more municipal taxes-all of which are indicators of the wealthier individual-he would receive greater benefit under this proposal. I would go further and say that in general terms this motion is contrary to the provisions and the spirit of our tax law.

October 26, 1973
Income Tax Rebate
[ Translation]
The Income Tax Act now grants abatements or, to use a more common expression, tax credits, only when it is established that the income received by the taxpayer has already been taxed. It is called the Foreign Tax Credit and it applies when the taxpayer gets from abroad an income that was taxed in the other country. The Income Tax Act then provides for a credit to be applied against Canadian taxes for an amount not exceeding that paid to the foreign country.

That is one of the few exceptions under the foreign tax credit where we do permit one area of taxation to be credited against another area of tax payable. The proposal in the motion of the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) goes even further. Essentially it argues that although an individual has not spent money pursuant to a business, or an adventure in the nature of trade, if I recall the expression used in the Income Tax Act, he will none the less be entitled to deduct from his income tax that amount of money which he has spent for his comfort.
While it is understood that a home is essential, it is an essential that does not have to be purchased. So the result of the motion would be very considerably to favour the individual who has adequate funds to buy a home and to leave out in the cold, so to speak, those individuals who choose not to buy or cannot afford a home in that they would not receive an equal or similar advantage in regard to their own income tax which is payable.
The question I might turn to next is that of specific examples within the income tax system itself as to how such a motion might apply to various individuals paying income tax. I know other members of the House wish to speak on this motion and I think it would be better to restrict my comments to the more general aspects of this question, as I have been doing up to now. I should like to mention one or two areas which I think are of interest. This motion would very substantially run counter, in its present form, to a similar idea which has been found workable in the provinces of Manitoba and Ontario. [Translation]
Incidentally, I wish to note that, in co-operation with the federal government, the two provinces I mentioned, Manitoba and Ontario, have established a tax-credit program in order to ease the local taxpayer's burden. But as for its big four original features, the program was first conceived so as to bring as much relief as possible to people on low income.
[ English]
That is in considerable contraction with the present motion which does not seem to assist those in the lower revenue brackets but, rather, those in the higher revenue brackets.
[ Translation]
Then, the provincial tax is reduced rather than the federal tax, so that provinces subsidize their own municipalities. Furthermore, provincial programs help both tenants and owners.

The present motion does not go to the question of what taxation aid might be given.

Finally, we pay money directly to the people involved when the credit is greater than the amount of income tax to be paid.

Therefore, for the general reasons I have mentioned- and I am led to believe that other speakers may wish to go into specific details in terms of actual taxation concepts-I would be opposed to the hon. member's motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know it is rather strange that I should rise to support the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) on this motion. However, I do so for two purposes. The first is so he can have the motion brought on and, second, because I think he has introduced into this House today a concept which is not new but which would, if adopted, provide a new form of relief and incentive to those in our society who to a greater and greater extent are concerned about housing. I think this is perhaps an even more important reason than the first one.
I am not terribly shocked to learn that the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore (Mr. Blaker) takes exception to what I might describe as a progressive proposal in respect of housing, because in dealing with housing the government he supports is notorious for its dinosaur attitude in respect of new innovations in this field. When we are speaking about a conference to which the minister can go and talk about new methods of bringing forth better housing for more Canadians, then of course the minister and members of his party are great at talking. When they have the instruments of power in their hands to provide some relief from this dreadful shortage in a land of plenty, there is a superabundance of talk and a poverty of progressive action in housing.
I rise today to support this motion as I think, contrary to what the hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore says, it will not provide relief for the very limited wealthy class in Canada but as wage rates increase it will provide a measure of relief, incentive and hope in Canada for those who find themselves in the middle income group which has been burdened to a greater extent by the tax load of modern society. This is not a new concept. On April 9, 1973, on motion of the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour), a Progressive Conservative member, and later on May 14, 1973, on motion of the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Morgan) this matter, in terms somewhat different though nonetheless consistent with the motion of the hon. member for Portneuf, was discussed by members of this party in the House.
I say as a matter of faith in this party that we are dedicated to the first principle that housing is a universal need; and the fact that homeownership is too expensive in Canada, a land of plenty in the 1970s, makes it a matter for government action and government priority. It is significant, in terms of considering the extent to which housing is a priority to this government, to realize that even at this late date, in spite of all the urging upon the government, it has refused to take off the 11 per cent sales tax on building

October 26, 1973

materials. This is a most regressive tax. This government has also refused to follow the lead of the province of Ontario in establishing a ministry of housing as a regular government department reporting to its own standing committee of this House.
I do not have to convince hon. members of the House who want to see that there is a problem, and I do not have to convince members of the House who care to see that this government has not really progressed very far in spite of its talk, its press releases and its propaganda regarding the position it takes on housing. It has been established that 80 per cent of Canadian families want to live in single-family dwellings. If 80 per cent want to do that, it is the duty of this government to provide the opportunity. The proposal of the hon. member for Portneuf would effect a dramatic reduction in the cost of housing for Canadian families, perhaps to the extent of almost $1 billion per year. The deductibility of mortgage interest rates would reduce the impact of inflation, of land and construction costs and of interest rates which over the past ten years, partly through errors of omission and partly through errors of commission by this government, have been far out of proportion to the general increase in the cost of living, but all of which have increased the cost of housing.
Let me refer as one example to the recent report on housing in the Toronto area. Housing in that area now costs 11 per cent more than it did one year ago. While food costs rise, people still eat; while clothing costs rise, people are still clothed. But an increase in housing costs deprives many Canadians of the prospect of home ownership and commits them to a life of paying rent.
I had the privilege of going through a number of high-rise buildings in my area during the course of the last election campaign. I have told this story on the floor of the House before. I met a young couple one night in the course of campaigning who told me they were saving money. The young fellow had a position in an institution here, a position of trust, and was managing to save money. But to use his words, he felt imprisoned in that apartment building. He was one of those who wanted to get into a home of his own and to bring his family up in that atmosphere.
There are others who do not, and I respect their wishes in that regard. However, the overwhelming number of Canadians wish to have a home of their own. Under the present situation, with inflation which is running rampant without control in this country, with the regressive taxes on building materials, and with a government which refuses to tackle the number one social problem in this country, thousands of Canadians will find themselves continually imprisoned in apartment buildings. I have never forgotten what that young person told me. We all know the main components in the cost of a house are the land upon which the house is built, the construction of the dwelling and the cost of the money. I believe it is fair to say the largest single cost contributor in recent years has been the cost of money in respect of the building and ownership of a home. It is primarily to that I understand the motion of the hon. member is directed, namely, the cost of financing a home.
Income Tax Rebate
I should like to give an example to illustrate how expensive this cost is. The rise in the interest rate from about 6 per cent to about 9 per cent, and now even higher, has added more to the monthly payment of an average mortgage loan than the average $5,000 increase in the price of a building lot would have added without a change in the interest rate. For example, a mortgage with a principal amount of $16,500 payable over a period of 25 years at 6 per cent would have a total interest cost of $15,200. The same mortgage, with principal of $16,500, carrying interest at the rate of 9 per cent, would have a total interest cost of $24,500, a difference in interest cost of $9,300 on a mortgage loan of $16,500. Furthermore, high interest rates may be substantially raising the level of annual income needed to secure a mortgage, compared with previous years. It is to that phenomenon that the motion of the hon. member is directed.
The hon. member for Lachine-Lakeshore seemed to say that this motion, worded as it was, could apply only to a single-family home. I have read the motion and am afraid I cannot apply to it that very restrictive interpretation; but I am not surprised that the hon. member has been able to do so, because he belongs to a very restrictive party. However, I have read the motion and it is possible under it to grant an income tax rebate equal to the amount paid in the form of mortgage interest on a family home. I think in our society it is possible, with the development of condominiums-some condominiums such as high-rise buildings and other condominiums of perhaps lower rise-for people to have a family home of this type.
The motion also deals with the provision of a reduction or rebate in respect of municipal taxes which a condominium owner would have to pay. Surely the motion is not so restrictive that it could not apply also to that proportion of the rent. It represents an increase in the rent paid by a renter of an apartment building as opposed to a condominium where the municipal taxes become part of the monthly payments in respect of that building. It would seem to me that such a provision would be of great advantage to people who rent. This is a unique attack and I know this government is not prepared particularly to accept a unique attack on anything, even on itself. However, it is an attack on one part of the spectrum, the difficulty that faces Canadians in all parts of this country. This will continue to be a problem facing Canadians to a greater and greater degree as they become more urbanized. This is part, not all, of the attack which must be made on what I believe is Canada's number one social problem.
I, for one, believe that how we solve the housing problems of Canadians, which have reached astronomical proportions, will be reflected in how this and other governments in Canada generally meet the social problems that will affect us as our society changes. We talk about many things, such as crimes in the streets, respect by children for their families and the breakdown of the family. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, I believe with great conviction that at the root of many of those problems is the inadequacy of housing and the variety of housing available for Canadian needs.
I shudder, frankly, to think of the communities we will be developing as we move into the latter part of the 1970s. In a few years, 85 per cent of all Canadians will live in an

October 26, 1973
Income Tax Rebate
area along the St. Lawrence River and in the major cities generally between Windsor and Montreal. I shudder to think of the problems that will develop when we continue to pack more and more people into fewer and fewer acres. I shudder to think what will happen in respect of our educational system which will suffer as a result of this development, with teachers teaching larger and larger classes. The burdens which are being placed on the municipalities in respect of recreation are horrendous, in my view, and I have had some experience in another capacity with regard to municipalities.
The problems generated by not attacking the housing problem are things I do not look forward to seeing. These are the things that are at the root of a national housing policy. The hon. member for Portneuf is not saying his motion is the be-all and end-all of a national housing policy. But I think he is saying, and I agree with him, that it is the beginning of a concrete plan for a real attack on this problem. Of course, it will cost the treasury money. I tend to think rather progressively, however, in respect to the future of Canada, and I believe that despite the inability of this government, notwithstanding its backwardlooking attitude and notwithstanding that it would rather restrict than give incentive, this country is capable of moving ahead and providing this kind of incentive to Canadians to own their own homes.
In the debate of April 9, 1973, myriad reasons were given by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Leblanc), speaking for the government, concerning why we should not venture into this kind of thing. I read that speech with absolute dismay. But having sat in this House since April 9 and having watched the government in action when dealing with other matters, I am not surprised as I read the speech again. This government has tended to put thumbs down on every practical idea that has come forward except those it can steal for its own advantage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief: nevertheless I would like to make a few comments on the motion before us.
People are now talking about an income tax rebate of $1,000. I often heard that some were considering reducing the income tax by the amount paid in taxes and interest. Now, I think this is going beyond all bounds: it is no longer a question of a rebate but of a tax reduction of $1,000.
I believe this policy would favour the wealthier people, those who own houses worth $50,000, $60,000, $75,000 or even $100,000, while we, in the Liberal party, are working very hard to try to help the Canadian worker who, through his labour, contributes to the development of Canada. Often, this Canadian worker who earns maybe only $8,000 a year owns a small and very modest house for which taxes and interests amount to only $500. In other words, this worker would be unable to save $500 contrarily to much richer people.
There are also the tenants who pay rent and cannot benefit from this tax deduction because they do not own the house. I know several people who are tenants in Montreal or Toronto but who own a $100,000 cottage in the north. And we would like to grant them a $1,000 tax deduction? I fail to see the rationale of this policy.
Furthermore, the people who own properties in Canada have an advantage that I would like to point out. They can make capital gains. Such gains are not taxable, not even at 50 per cent because there is an exemption for the main residence. This is in itself an advantage and we would like the federal government to give them $1,000 more. Finally, if that policy were implemented for income tax returns we would have to hire a few more civil servants as it would be necessary to increase control over income tax returns.
I think we should concentrate on the creation of productive employment so that our national gross product continue to grow and that would increase our exportations since our Canadian dollar is high on the international market.
But the more we create-what I call non-productive jobs-I would not say unnecessary-we weaken our Canadian dollar. In his motion, the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin) compares this deduction with the income deductions for foreigners. I wish to point out to my colleague that these same deductions are also applied in other countries and that after all we do not lose a cent. He also compares these deductions with the deductions on dividends. These deductions on dividends, Mr. Speaker, are only intended to avoid double taxation, because the company before paying a dividend has already paid taxes. If that amount became taxable a second time, the taxpayer would be subject to double taxation. Therefore, I do not see any relation.
It has often been stated, in support of that measure, that the owners of income-producing properties are entitled to deduct their taxes, their heating costs and their insurance. But we must understand something: Before being entitled to deduct those expenses, the taxpayer must firstly state
October 26, 1973

his income in his return and then he can deduct his expenses. Normally, someone who buys an income-producing property does so to realize profits. The taxpayer must finally pay more taxes. Moreover, if he could reduce his income to a depreciation expenditure, it would be useless because since January 1, 1972, depreciation expenditures can no longer be claimed as a loss.
One last point I would like to make is that I have some feeling that this policy would also run counter to provincial laws. We often hear about autonomy, that the federal government interferes with provincial and even municipal policies. I think this is a case where we would really interfere with municipal administration.
Finally, I would like to suggest that direct taxes, sales taxes and municipal levies are one of the most equitable means of taxation because we know that in Canada today, even though we have an excellent Income Tax Branch, many people manage to evade taxes. And one thing is certain, it is that direct taxes have to be paid even by tax evaders and this is at least one aspect of justice from which Canadians benefit.
