Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of speaking on this matter. However, in view of the irresponsible statements made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) I feel obliged to bring forward facts which are indisputable. What I find most regrettable in the remarks of the hon. member is that he said this government has not advanced in the matter of housing.
I wish to inform the hon. member that in my latest discussions with the manager of CMHC in the city of North Bay I have found that the response from the public in my riding to the recent amendments to the NHA, including the home assistance plan, has contributed to making that office the busiest it has been for years. It is helping to increase the number of construction starts of homes and apartments in my riding so that we expect there will be an approximate increase of 20 per cent over the housing starts of the past year. I want, further, to indicate that according to the latest estimate there will be up to 250,000 housing starts in the next four years. This is contemplated as continuing because of the encouragement given to the housing market by the progressive policies adopted by this government. The new housing starts that will take place in the next few years and that have taken place since 1968 also point out the untenable position adopted by the mover and seconder of this motion.
If we envisage an increase in housing starts of 250,000 in the next four years, it means that for every four years we will be losing $1 billion in tax revenue, as we have indeed since 1969. When we consider that housing starts since that time have gone up by nearly 10 per cent, we see that in the past four years we have suffered a loss of $1 billion in revenue. When we consider that the total federal budget this year is $18 billion, we see quite clearly the percentage of income and revenue which would be lost as a result of this suggested measure being adopted.
Income Tax Rebate
I would suggest that such absence of extra revenue would mean the government would be looking for additional funds in order to assist people who do not have adequate housing. It would not have been able to implement those programs which are now receiving such popular acclaim, and indeed it would have depressed the labour market in the construction field and the construction industry itself, which could have had very serious results.
Mr. Speaker, I wished to say only a few words to set the record straight on those particular issues. I thank you for your attention.

That is true, but anyone in Canada receiving an income of $10,000 a year can take up the $1,600 or $1,800 which is more than is proposed in the motion before us. So in Canada a large income is not needed in order to take advantage of the saving in income tax through a registered savings plan. If we look at the over-all perspective, it is apparent that Canadians enjoy a substantial benefit through their contributions to pension plans even though they are not allowed to extend these savings to mortgage interest.
When the Royal Commission on Taxation thoroughly reviewed the income tax system several years ago, it recommended that the principle of not allowing a deduction for personal or living expenses be retained. It did not recommend a deduction for municipal taxes or mortgage interest. When tax reform was introduced, it was recognized that the encouragement of home ownership was desirable. On the other hand, it was thought best not to deviate from the basic rule regarding deductibility of personal expenses.

October 26, 1973
Income Tax Rebate
The Income Tax Act, therefore, provided two major incentives to home ownership. The first incentive was to allow a taxpayer to make a capital gain on the sale of his home without incurring tax liability. This is something, of course, that is not available to the person who rents an apartment. The second was to continue the practice of not including in the taxpayer's income the economic benefit which he receives from home ownership. This benefit, which is the value of his accommodation, may be looked upon as the return he has received on the capital he has invested. It is interesting to note in passing that other countries, including Great Britain, have added this imputed income to the taxpayer's income for tax purposes in years gone by.
I should like to look at two or three examples of how the hon. member's proposal would work. Let us look, first, at the taxpayer who has an income of $5,000. His federal taxes in 1972 would be $85, and his provincial taxes if he lived in Ontario would be about $26, totalling $111. If he had municipal taxes of $200 and interest payments of $800, it would appear that he would be entitled to a rebate of $1,000. However, the hon. member's motion speaks of a rebate against income tax. The federal government would
give him a credit of $85 and his tax bill would be nil. At the same time, because provincial taxes are calculated as a percentage of federal taxes, his provincial tax rate would be nil. The total benefit which the taxpayer received would be only $111, or just over 11 per cent of the expenses in connection with his house, and of this amount $26 would have been contributed by the province in which he lived.
Now let us look at a taxpayer in a higher income bracket who owns his home and has no mortgage. He lives in a very expensive home and the municipal taxes are $1,000 per year. He gets the benefit of a tax deduction of $1,000 from the federal government, and $305 from the provincial government. In effect, he has made a tax-free profit of $305, or 30.5 per cent simply by paying his municipal taxes. These examples demonstrate some key propositions. The rebate would favour the higher income taxpayer over the lower income taxpayer.
